You work at a bank and have a custom tabular ML model supplied by the bank’s vendor. Its training data is unavailable because it is sensitive. The model is packaged in a Vertex AI Model serving container that accepts one string per prediction instance, with feature values in each string separated by commas.  
  
You want to deploy this model to production for online predictions and, with minimal effort, monitor how the feature distribution changes over time. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Upload the model to Vertex AI Model Registry, and deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint2. Create a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job with feature drift detection as the monitoring objective, and provide an instance schema

1. Upload the model to Vertex AI Model Registry, and deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint2. Create a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job with feature skew detection as the monitoring objective, and provide an instance schema

1. Refactor the serving container to accept key-value pairs as input format2. Upload the model to Vertex AI Model Registry, and deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint3. Create a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job with feature drift detection as the monitoring objective.

1. Refactor the serving container to accept key-value pairs as input format2. Upload the model to Vertex AI Model Registry, and deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint3. Create a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job with feature skew detection as the monitoring objective

questions.explanation:
Feature drift detects changes in feature distributions in production data over time and does not require the unavailable training dataset as a reference. For a custom model receiving CSV-string inputs, an analysis instance schema specifies the payload format, feature names, types, and feature order, allowing Model Monitoring to parse those inputs without changing the serving container. Feature skew instead compares serving data with training data, so it is unsuitable when the training data is unavailable.

**Learn more:** [Provide schemas to Vertex AI Model Monitoring](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/model-monitoring/schemas)

You are developing a model to predict daily temperatures. You randomly split the data and then transformed the training and test datasets. Temperature data for model training is uploaded hourly. During testing, the model achieved 97% accuracy; however, after deployment to production, its accuracy fell to 66%. How can you improve the production model’s accuracy?

options.text: Normalize the data for the training, and test datasets as two separate steps.
Split the training and test data based on time rather than a random split to avoid leakage.
Add more data to your test set to ensure that you have a fair distribution and sample for testing.
Apply data transformations before splitting, and cross-validate to make sure that the transformations are applied to both the training and test sets.

questions.explanation: Temperature observations are time-series data, so randomly splitting them can leak future or closely related observations into the training set and inflate offline accuracy. Splitting chronologically evaluates the model on later, unseen periods in the same way production does, yielding a more reliable model assessment and reducing temporal leakage.

options.text: 1. Upload the audio files to Cloud Storage2. Call the speech:longrunningrecognize API endpoint to generate transcriptions3. Call the predict method of an AutoML sentiment analysis model to analyze the transcriptions.

questions.explanation:

A Cloud Function can automate that downstream analysis.

You are training an object-detection model on a Cloud TPU v2, but training is taking longer than expected. Based on this simplified trace from a Cloud TPU profile, what action should you take to reduce training time cost-effectively?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783824537298-b0jexocx.png)

options.text: Move from Cloud TPU v2 to Cloud TPU v3 and increase batch size.
Move from Cloud TPU v2 to 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs and increase batch size.
Rewrite your input function to resize and reshape the input images.
Rewrite your input function using parallel reads, parallel processing, and prefetch.

questions.explanation:
The workload is input-bound: data extraction, transformation, and network loading occur before each TPU training interval, leaving the TPU idle while it waits for the next batch. Parallel file reads and preprocessing, together with prefetching, overlap input preparation with training and keep the TPU supplied with data without requiring more expensive accelerator hardware. Google Cloud recommends parallel reads, parallel `map()` calls, and `prefetch()` to mitigate TPU input-processing bottlenecks.

**Learn more:** [Cloud TPU performance guide](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/performance-guide) · [Troubleshooting TensorFlow on Cloud TPU](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/troubleshooting/trouble-tf)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are training an object-detection machine learning model using a dataset of three million X-ray images, each approximately 2 GB in size. You use Vertex AI Training to run a custom training application on a Compute Engine instance with 32 cores, 128 GB of RAM, and one NVIDIA P100 GPU. You observe that model training is taking a very long time. You want to reduce the training time without compromising model performance. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the instance memory to 512 GB, and increase the batch size.
Replace the NVIDIA P100 GPU with a K80 GPU in the training job.
Enable early stopping in your Vertex AI Training job.
Use the tf.distribute.Strategy API and run a distributed training job.

questions.explanation:
Distributed training divides data-parallel training work across multiple workers and GPUs, reducing wall-clock training time while preserving the training objective. Vertex AI supports distributed TensorFlow training with the `tf.distribute.Strategy` API, including multi-worker strategies that coordinate data distribution and gradient updates across machines.

**Learn more:** [Distributed training | Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/distributed-training)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a retail company and are responsible for developing an ML model that predicts product sales. The company’s historical sales data is stored in BigQuery and contains features such as date, store location, product category, and promotion details. You need to select the most effective combination of a BigQuery ML model and feature engineering to maximize prediction accuracy. What should you do?

options.text: Use a linear regression model. Perform one-hot encoding on categorical features, and create additional features based on the date, such as day of the week or month.
Use a boosted tree model. Perform label encoding on categorical features, and transform the date column into numeric values.
Use an autoencoder model. Perform label encoding on categorical features, and normalize the date column.
Use a matrix factorization model. Perform one-hot encoding on categorical features, and create interaction features between the store location and product category variables.

questions.explanation:
Product-sales prediction is a regression problem. A BigQuery ML boosted tree regressor is well suited to tabular data with nonlinear relationships and interactions among promotions, stores, categories, and time. BigQuery ML supports boosted-tree regression and supports label encoding for nonnumeric categorical features; label encoding is the default categorical encoding method for boosted-tree models. Autoencoders are unsupervised, while matrix factorization is not the appropriate general-purpose model for this regression task.

**Learn more:** [Regression overview | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/regression-overview) · [The CREATE MODEL statement for boosted trees models using XGBoost | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/bigqueryml-syntax-create-boosted-tree)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An ML model was deployed to production one year ago. Each month, you collect all raw requests sent to the model prediction service during the prior month. You send a subset of those requests to a human labeling service to assess the model’s performance.  
  
After one year, you observe that model performance sometimes degrades substantially after a month, whereas at other times it takes several months to detect a performance decrease. The labeling service is expensive, but large performance degradations must also be avoided. You need to decide how often to retrain the model in order to maintain high performance while minimizing cost. What should you do?

options.text: Train an anomaly detection model on the training dataset, and run all incoming requests through this model. If an anomaly is detected, send the most recent serving data to the labeling service.
Identify temporal patterns in your model’s performance over the previous year. Based on these patterns, create a schedule for sending serving data to the labeling service for the next year.

Compare the cost of the labeling service with the lost revenue due to model performance degradation over the past year. If the lost revenue is greater than the cost of the labeling service, increase the frequency of model retraining; otherwise, decrease the model retraining frequency.

Run training-serving skew detection batch jobs every few days to compare the aggregate statistics of the features in the training dataset with recent serving data. If skew is detected, send the most recent serving data to the labeling service.

questions.explanation:
Training-serving skew detection compares aggregate feature distributions in recent serving data with the training-data baseline, allowing potential data-distribution changes to be identified before paying to obtain labels. Running these checks frequently and sending recent serving data to human labeling only when skew is detected focuses the expensive performance evaluation and subsequent retraining decisions on periods where degradation is more likely.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/ai-platform/docs/technical-overview) · [Provide schemas to Vertex AI Model Monitoring](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/model-monitoring/schemas)

You recently built a deep learning model with Keras and are now trying different training strategies. You initially trained the model on a single GPU, but training was too slow. You then distributed training over 4 GPUs with `tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy` (making no other changes), but did not see a reduction in training time. What should you do?

options.text: Distribute the dataset with tf.distribute.Strategy.experimental_distribute_dataset
Create a custom training loop.
Use a TPU with tf.distribute.TPUStrategy.
Increase the batch size.

questions.explanation:
`tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy` divides the global batch among the GPU replicas. Increasing the global batch size lets each GPU process a sufficiently large per-replica batch, making better use of the additional compute capacity; the learning rate may also need retuning.

**Learn more:** [Distributed training with TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/distributed_training) · [Distributed training with Keras](https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/distribute/keras)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have recently built a custom neural-network model for image classification. You need to automatically determine the values for learning rate, number of layers, and kernel size. To accomplish this, you plan to run multiple jobs in parallel to identify the parameters that optimize performance. You want to minimize custom-code development and infrastructure management. What should you do?

options.text: Train an AutoML image classification model.
Create a custom training job that uses the Vertex AI Vizier SDK for parameter optimization.
Create a Vertex AI hyperparameter tuning job.
Create a Vertex AI pipeline that runs different model training jobs in parallel.

questions.explanation:
A Vertex AI hyperparameter tuning job runs trials of a custom training job using different hyperparameter values, evaluates the configured optimization metric, and supports a specified number of trials running in parallel. This provides managed hyperparameter search without building custom orchestration or managing the underlying training infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Vertex AI HyperparameterTuningJob REST resource](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/reference/rest/v1/projects.locations.hyperparameterTuningJobs) · [Create a Vertex AI hyperparameter tuning job](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/samples/aiplatform-create-hyperparameter-tuning-job-sample)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an AI text generator that can dynamically adapt its responses to reflect a user's writing style and imitate famous authors when their style is detected. You have a large dataset containing works by various authors, and plan to host the model on a custom VM. You want to use the most effective model. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy Llama 3 from Model Garden, and use prompt engineering techniques.
Fine-tune a BERT-based model from TensorFlow Hub.
Fine-tune Llama 3 from Model Garden on Vertex AI Pipelines.
Use the Gemini 1.5 Flash foundational model to build the text generator.

questions.explanation:
Fine-tuning a generative LLM on a large corpus of authorial writing adapts its weights to the stylistic patterns in that data, producing more consistent style-conditioned text than prompt engineering alone. BERT is primarily an encoder model for language understanding rather than autoregressive text generation. Vertex AI Model Garden supports fine-tunable models through custom notebooks or pipelines and supports deployment workflows for open models.

**Learn more:** [Overview of Model Garden](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/model-garden/explore-models) · [Introduction to tuning](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/models/tune-models)

You work for a gaming company that creates massively multiplayer online (MMO) games. You built a TensorFlow model that predicts whether players will make in-app purchases of more than $10 during the next two weeks. The model’s predictions will be used to tailor each user’s game experience. User data is stored in BigQuery. How should you serve the model while optimizing cost, user experience, and ease of management?

options.text: Import the model into BigQuery ML. Make predictions using batch reading data from BigQuery, and push the data to Cloud SQL
Deploy the model to Vertex AI Prediction. Make predictions using batch reading data from Cloud Bigtable, and push the data to Cloud SQL.
Embed the model in the mobile application. Make predictions after every in-app purchase event is published in Pub/Sub, and push the data to Cloud SQL.
Embed the model in the streaming Dataflow pipeline. Make predictions after every in-app purchase event is published in Pub/Sub, and push the data to Cloud SQL.

questions.explanation:
A streaming Dataflow pipeline can consume each in-app purchase event from Pub/Sub, run TensorFlow inference within the pipeline, and persist the updated prediction to Cloud SQL for the game application. This provides timely event-driven personalization while keeping inference centrally managed and avoiding per-device model distribution. Dataflow ML supports TensorFlow inference in streaming pipelines through Apache Beam’s `RunInference` transform.

**Learn more:** [About Dataflow ML](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/machine-learning/ml-about) · [Read from Pub/Sub to Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/streaming-with-cloud-pubsub)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are training an LSTM-based model on AI Platform to summarize text with the following job-submission script:  
  
```bash  
gcloud ai-platform jobs submit training $JOB_NAME \  
--package-path $TRAINER_PACKAGE_PATH \  
--module-name $MAIN_TRAINER_MODULE \  
--job-dir $JOB_DIR \  
--region $REGION \  
--scale-tier basic \  
-- \  
--epochs 20 \  
--batch_size=32 \  
--learning_rate=0.001 \  
```  
  
You want to ensure that training time is minimized without significantly compromising your model’s accuracy. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the 'epochs' parameter.
Modify the 'scale-tier' parameter.
Modify the 'batch size' parameter.
Modify the 'learning rate' parameter.

questions.explanation:
The AI Platform `scale-tier` setting controls the compute configuration, including machine types and the number of worker and parameter-server replicas. The `basic` tier uses a single worker, whereas other tiers can supply greater or distributed compute capacity, reducing training time without directly changing the model’s learning behavior or accuracy target.

**Learn more:** [gcloud ai-platform jobs submit training](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai-platform/jobs/submit/training)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You developed a Transformer model in TensorFlow to translate text. Your training data includes millions of documents in a Cloud Storage bucket. You plan to use distributed training to reduce the training time. You need to configure the training job while minimizing the effort needed to modify code and manage the cluster configuration. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Vertex AI custom training job with GPU accelerators for the second worker pool. Use tf.distribute.MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy for distribution.

Create a Vertex AI custom distributed training job with Reduction Server. Use N1 high-memory machine type instances for the first and second pools, and use N1 high-CPU machine type instances for the third worker pool.
Create a training job that uses Cloud TPU VMs. Use tf.distribute.TPUStrategy for distribution.
Create a Vertex AI custom training job with a single worker pool of A2 GPU machine type instances. Use tf.distribute.MirroredStrategv for distribution.

questions.explanation:
`tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy` provides synchronous data-parallel training across the multiple GPUs attached to one machine. A single Vertex AI worker pool using an A2 GPU machine avoids multi-worker cluster configuration while requiring only minimal changes to make the TensorFlow model strategy-aware.

**Learn more:** [TensorFlow distributed training guide](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/distributed_training) · [tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy API reference](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/distribute/MirroredStrategy)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a delivery company and must design a system to store and manage features such as delivered parcels and truck locations over time. The system must retrieve these features with low latency and supply them to a model for online prediction. The data science team will retrieve historical data at a specific point in time for model training. You want to store the features with minimal effort. What should you do?

options.text: Store features in Bigtable as key/value data.
Store features in Vertex AI Feature Store.
Store features as a Vertex AI dataset, and use those features to train the models hosted in Vertex AI endpoints.
Store features in BigQuery timestamp partitioned tables, and use the BigQuery Storage Read API to serve the features.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Feature Store is a managed feature-management service that supports low-latency online serving for real-time predictions and offline retrieval of historical feature values, including point-in-time data for model training. It therefore satisfies both serving and training requirements while minimizing infrastructure-management effort.

**Learn more:** [Feature serving | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/feature-serving) · [Feature Store overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/machine-learning/featurestore/latest/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an ML recommendation model for shoppers on your company’s ecommerce website. You will use Recommendations AI to build, test, and deploy the system. How should you develop recommendations that increase revenue while following best practices?

options.text: Use the ג€Other Products You May Likeג€ recommendation type to increase the click-through rate.
Use the ג€Frequently Bought Togetherג€ recommendation type to increase the shopping cart size for each order.
Import your user events and then your product catalog to make sure you have the highest quality event stream.
Because it will take time to collect and record product data, use placeholder values for the product catalog to test the viability of the model.

questions.explanation:
Frequently Bought Together recommends complementary items that are commonly purchased in the same shopping session. It is designed for shopping-cart expansion and optimizes revenue by increasing the likelihood of items being added to carts, which can raise order value.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You trained a TensorFlow DNN regressor to predict housing prices from predictive features. Your default precision is `tf.float64`, and you use a standard TensorFlow estimator:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783828037012-z4zh59re.png)  
  
The model performs well, but immediately before production deployment you find that serving latency is **10 ms at the 90th percentile** and that you currently serve on CPUs. Production requires model latency of **8 ms at the 90th percentile**. You are willing to accept a small reduction in performance to meet the latency requirement.  
  
Therefore, you plan to improve latency while evaluating the amount by which the model's predictions decrease. What should you try first to quickly reduce serving latency?

options.text: Switch from CPU to GPU serving.
Apply quantization to your SavedModel by reducing the floating point precision to tf.float16.
Increase the dropout rate to 0.8 and retrain your model.
Increase the dropout rate to 0.8 in _PREDICT mode by adjusting the TensorFlow Serving parameters.

questions.explanation:
Post-training quantization reduces numerical precision without retraining, shrinking the model and reducing inference computation and memory use; any resulting prediction-quality change can be evaluated after conversion. TensorFlow documents post-training quantization as a technique to reduce model size and improve latency, and float16 quantization is intended to incur minimal accuracy loss.

**Learn more:** [TensorFlow Model Optimization: Post-training quantization](https://www.tensorflow.org/model_optimization/guide/quantization/post_training)

questions.question: You are developing a binary-classification ML algorithm that determines whether an image of a classified scanned document contains a company’s logo. In the dataset, 96% of examples lack the logo, making the dataset highly skewed. Which metrics would provide the greatest confidence in the model?

options.text: F-score where recall is weighed more than precision
RMSE
F1 score
F-score where precision is weighed more than recall

questions.explanation: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it evaluates positive-logo detection without allowing the overwhelmingly common no-logo class to dominate the result. It gives equal importance to avoiding false positives and false negatives when neither error type is specified as more important.

questions.question: You are developing a binary-classification ML algorithm that determines whether an image of a classified scanned document contains a company’s logo. In the dataset, 96% of examples lack the logo, making the dataset highly skewed. Which metrics would provide the greatest confidence in the model?

options.text: An optimization objective that minimizes Log loss
An optimization objective that maximizes the Precision at a Recall value of 0.50
An optimization objective that maximizes the area under the precision-recall curve (AUC PR) value
An optimization objective that maximizes the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC ROC) value

questions.explanation:
Precision measures the proportion of transactions predicted as fraudulent that are actually fraudulent, so maximizing precision minimizes false positives. The Precision at Recall objective maximizes that precision while maintaining the selected recall level for detecting fraud. Google Cloud documents this objective as optimizing precision at a specific recall value.

**Learn more:** [Train a model with End-to-End AutoML — Optimization objectives](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/tabular-workflows/e2e-automl-train)

options.text: Set up a Vertex AI Workbench instance with a Spark kernel.
Use Colab Enterprise with a Spark kernel.
Set up a Dataproc cluster with Spark and use Jupyter notebooks.
Configure a Compute Engine instance with Spark and use Jupyter notebooks.

questions.explanation:
A Spark-enabled Vertex AI Workbench instance supplies managed JupyterLab and includes the Dataproc JupyterLab extension, which lets notebooks run Apache Spark workloads through remote Spark kernels on Dataproc. This minimizes infrastructure setup while supporting large-scale Spark-based prototyping.

**Learn more:** [Create a Dataproc Spark-enabled Vertex AI Workbench instance](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/workbench/instances/create-dataproc-enabled)

You recently developed the first version of an image-segmentation model for a self-driving car. After deploying it, you notice a decline in the area-under-the-curve (AUC) metric. While reviewing video recordings, you also find that the model fails in highly congested traffic but works as expected when traffic is lighter. What is the most likely cause of this outcome?

options.text: The model is overfitting in areas with less traffic and underfitting in areas with more traffic.
AUC is not the correct metric to evaluate this classification model.
Too much data representing congested areas was used for model training.
Gradients become small and vanish while backpropagating from the output to input nodes.

questions.explanation: Condition-specific performance in which a model succeeds in less-complex traffic scenes but fails in highly congested scenes is consistent with overfitting to lower-traffic patterns and inadequate fitting or generalization for the more complex congested-traffic distribution.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a large bank that serves customers through an application hosted in Google Cloud and running in the US and Singapore. You developed a PyTorch model that classifies transactions as potentially fraudulent or not. The model is a three-layer perceptron that takes both numerical and categorical features as input, with hashing performed within the model.  
  
You deployed the model in the `us-central1` region on `nl-highcpu-16` machines, with predictions served in real time. The model’s current median response latency is 40 ms. You want to lower latency, particularly in Singapore, where some customers experience the longest delays. What should you do?

options.text: Attach an NVIDIA T4 GPU to the machines being used for online inference.
Change the machines being used for online inference to nl-highcpu-32.
Deploy the model to Vertex AI private endpoints in the us-central1 and asia-southeast1 regions, and allow the application to choose the appropriate endpoint.
Create another Vertex AI endpoint in the asia-southeast1 region, and allow the application to choose the appropriate endpoint.

questions.explanation:
Regional deployment places online inference close to the application workload, reducing cross-region network latency. Vertex AI endpoints are identified by project, region, and endpoint; private inference clients must be in the same region as the deployed model. Deploying private endpoints in both `us-central1` and `asia-southeast1` and routing requests to the appropriate regional endpoint minimizes the distance between each application deployment and its inference service.

**Learn more:** [Use private services access endpoints for online inference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/using-private-endpoints) · [gcloud ai endpoints reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/endpoints)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a linear model with more than 100 input features, each having values between –1 and 1. You believe that many features are non-informative. You want to remove non-informative features from the model while retaining informative features in their original form. Which technique should you use?

options.text: Use principal component analysis (PCA) to eliminate the least informative features.
Use L1 regularization to reduce the coefficients of uninformative features to 0.
After building your model, use Shapley values to determine which features are the most informative.
Use an iterative dropout technique to identify which features do not degrade the model when removed.

questions.explanation:
L1 regularization (such as Lasso) yields sparse linear models by setting many coefficients exactly to zero. The zero-coefficient features can be removed, while retained features remain the original input features rather than transformed components.

**Learn more:** [scikit-learn: Feature selection](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/feature_selection.html?highlight=lasso) · [scikit-learn: Linear models—Lasso](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html)

You are an ML engineer at a global car manufacturer. You must build an ML model that predicts car sales across different cities worldwide. Which features or feature crosses should you use to train city-specific relationships between car type and the number of sales?

options.text: Thee individual features: binned latitude, binned longitude, and one-hot encoded car type.
One feature obtained as an element-wise product between latitude, longitude, and car type.
One feature obtained as an element-wise product between binned latitude, binned longitude, and one-hot encoded car type.
Two feature crosses as an element-wise product: the first between binned latitude and one-hot encoded car type, and the second between binned longitude and one-hot encoded car type.

questions.explanation:
A city is identified by the conjunction of latitude and longitude, so both location values must be binned and crossed together. Crossing that joint location with the one-hot encoded car type produces separate features for each city-bin and car-type combination, allowing the model to learn city-specific sales relationships. Feature crosses are Cartesian products of categorical or bucketed features and encode their interactions.

**Learn more:** [Feature crosses — Google Machine Learning Crash Course](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/categorical-data/feature-crosses) · [Feature-cross assessment — Google Machine Learning Crash Course](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/MCE/mc-il-feature-crosses)

While profiling your TensorFlow model’s training time, you identify a performance problem caused by inefficiencies in the input data pipeline for a single 5-terabyte CSV-file dataset on Cloud Storage. You need to optimize input-pipeline performance. Which action should you try first to improve your pipeline’s efficiency?

options.text: Preprocess the input CSV file into a TFRecord file.
Randomly select a 10 gigabyte subset of the data to train your model.
Split into multiple CSV files and use a parallel interleave transformation.
Set the reshuffle_each_iteration parameter to true in the tf.data.Dataset.shuffle method.

questions.explanation:
Remote storage can provide high aggregate bandwidth, but reading one file may use only a small portion of it. Sharding the dataset into multiple sufficiently large CSV files enables concurrent reads; using parallel `Dataset.interleave` overlaps data loading and reduces input-processing time.

**Learn more:** [Better performance with the tf.data API](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/data_performance) · [TFRecord and tf.train.Example](https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/load_data/tfrecord)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have created unit tests for a Kubeflow Pipeline that depend on custom libraries. You want to automate running the unit tests for every new push to your development branch in Cloud Source Repositories. What should you do?

options.text: Write a script that sequentially performs the push to your development branch and executes the unit tests on Cloud Run.
Using Cloud Build, set an automated trigger to execute the unit tests when changes are pushed to your development branch.
Set up a Cloud Logging sink to a Pub/Sub topic that captures interactions with Cloud Source Repositories. Configure a Pub/Sub trigger for Cloud Run, and execute the unit tests on Cloud Run.

Set up a Cloud Logging sink to a Pub/Sub topic that captures interactions with Cloud Source Repositories. Execute the unit tests using a Cloud Function that is triggered when messages are sent to the Pub/Sub topic.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build triggers provide continuous-integration automation for source changes and can be configured to run on pushes to a specified Cloud Source Repositories branch. The build configuration can install the custom dependencies and execute the pipeline unit tests as build steps.

**Learn more:** [Automating builds with Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/source-repositories/docs/integrating-with-cloud-build) · [Create and manage build triggers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/automating-builds/create-manage-triggers)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building ML models with AI Platform for image segmentation of CT scans. You often revise your model architectures based on the latest available research papers and must rerun training on the same dataset to benchmark performance. You want to minimize computation costs and manual intervention while maintaining version control for your code. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Functions to identify changes to your code in Cloud Storage and trigger a retraining job.
Use the gcloud command-line tool to submit training jobs on AI Platform when you update your code.
Use Cloud Build linked with Cloud Source Repositories to trigger retraining when new code is pushed to the repository.
Create an automated workflow in Cloud Composer that runs daily and looks for changes in code in Cloud Storage using a sensor.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Build triggers can automatically start a build whenever code is pushed to a connected Cloud Source Repositories repository. A build configuration can submit the retraining job, providing an event-driven, version-controlled workflow without manual job submission or daily polling.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Build triggers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/triggers) · [Automating builds with Cloud Build](https://docs.cloud.google.com/source-repositories/docs/integrating-with-cloud-build)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an MLOps platform to automate your company’s ML experiments and model retraining. You need to organize artifacts for dozens of pipelines. How should you store the pipelines’ artifacts?

options.text: Store parameters in Cloud SQL, and store the models’ source code and binaries in GitHub.
Store parameters in Cloud SQL, store the models’ source code in GitHub, and store the models’ binaries in Cloud Storage.
Store parameters in Vertex ML Metadata, store the models’ source code in GitHub, and store the models’ binaries in Cloud Storage.
Store parameters in Vertex ML Metadata and store the models’ source code and binaries in GitHub.

questions.explanation:
Vertex ML Metadata records ML experiment parameters, artifacts, and lineage, making it appropriate for organizing and tracking pipeline metadata at scale. GitHub provides version control for model source code, while Cloud Storage is suitable for storing model binary artifacts.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to Vertex ML Metadata](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/ml-metadata/introduction) · [Cloud Storage documentation](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work on the AI team at an automobile company and are building a visual defect-detection model with TensorFlow and Keras. To improve model performance, you want to add image-augmentation functions such as translation, cropping, and contrast adjustment. These functions are randomly applied to every training batch. You want to optimize the data-processing pipeline for runtime and compute-resource utilization. What should you do?

options.text: Embed the augmentation functions dynamically in the tf.Data pipeline.
Embed the augmentation functions dynamically as part of Keras generators.
Use Dataflow to create all possible augmentations, and store them as TFRecords.
Use Dataflow to create the augmentations dynamically per training run, and stage them as TFRecords.

questions.explanation:
Dynamic augmentation in a `tf.data` pipeline keeps transformations in TensorFlow’s optimized input pipeline. `Dataset.map` can parallelize independent preprocessing work, and prefetching can overlap preprocessing with model execution. Generating augmentations on demand also avoids storing the large set of possible augmented-image TFRecords.

**Learn more:** [Better performance with the tf.data API](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/data_performance) · [tf.data: Build TensorFlow input pipelines](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/data)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are an ML researcher evaluating several deep learning model architectures and hyperparameter configurations. You need to implement a robust solution that tracks the progress of every model iteration, visualizes key metrics, provides insight into model internals, and optimizes training performance.  
  
You want the most efficient and powerful approach for comparing the models, with the strongest visualization capabilities. How should you build this solution?

options.text: Use Vertex AI TensorBoard for in-depth visualization and analysis, and use BigQuery for experiment tracking and analysis.
Use Vertex AI TensorBoard for visualizing training progress and model behavior, and use Vertex AI Feature Store to stove and manage experiment data for analysis and reproducibility.
Use Vertex AI Experiments for tracking iterations and comparison, and use Vertex AI TensorBoard for visualization and analysis of the training metrics and model architecture.
Use Vertex AI Experiments for tracking iterations and comparison, and use BigQuery and Looker Studio for visualization and analysis of the training metrics and model architecture.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Experiments tracks and compares model-development iterations by logging each experiment run’s inputs, parameters, artifacts, and metrics. Vertex AI TensorBoard provides detailed visualizations of training metrics and model graphs, and it supports training-performance profiling. Together, they address experiment comparison, model-internals analysis, and training optimization.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to Vertex AI Experiments](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/machine-learning/experiments/intro-vertex-ai-experiments) · [Introduction to Vertex AI TensorBoard](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/machine-learning/experiments/tensorboard-introduction)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You developed an ML model that detects sentiment in users’ posts on your company’s social-media page to identify outages or bugs. You use Dataflow to deliver real-time predictions for data ingested from Pub/Sub. You plan to train the model through multiple iterations and retain the newest two versions live after each run. You want traffic divided 80:20 between the versions, with the newest model receiving most traffic. You also want the simplest pipeline possible with minimal management. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the models to a Vertex AI endpoint using the traffic-split=0=80, PREVIOUS_MODEL_ID=20 configuration.
Wrap the models inside an App Engine application using the --splits PREVIOUS_VERSION=0.2, NEW_VERSION=0.8 configuration
Wrap the models inside a Cloud Run container using the REVISION1=20, REVISION2=80 revision configuration.
Implement random splitting in Dataflow using beam.Partition() with a partition function calling a Vertex AI endpoint.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI endpoints can serve multiple deployed models and route prediction traffic by percentage. In a deployment traffic split, `0` represents the newly deployed model, so `0=80, PREVIOUS_MODEL_ID=20` directs 80% of requests to the newest model while retaining the prior model for the remaining 20%.

**Learn more:** [Deploy a model on Vertex AI to get predictions](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/image-data/object-detection/get-predictions)

You have been asked to build a model using a dataset stored in a medium-sized (~10 GB) BigQuery table. You need to rapidly determine whether this data is appropriate for model development. You require maximum flexibility in creating the report. What should you do?

options.text: Use Vertex AI Workbench user-managed notebooks to generate the report.
Use the Google Data Studio to create the report.
Use the output from TensorFlow Data Validation on Dataflow to generate the report.
Use Dataprep to create the report.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for an online grocery store and recently developed a custom ML model that recommends a recipe when a user visits the website. You selected the machine type on the Vertex AI endpoint to optimize costs, using the queries per second (QPS) the model can serve, and deployed it on one machine with 8 vCPUs and no accelerators.  
  
A holiday season is coming, and you expect traffic to be four times the typical daily volume. You need to make sure the model can scale efficiently for the increased demand. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Maintain the same machine type on the endpoint.2. Set up a monitoring job and an alert for CPU usage.3. If you receive an alert, add a compute node to the endpoint.
1. Change the machine type on the endpoint to have 32 vCPUs.2. Set up a monitoring job and an alert for CPU usage.3. If you receive an alert, scale the vCPUs further as needed.

1. Maintain the same machine type on the endpoint Configure the endpoint to enable autoscaling based on vCPU usage.2. Set up a monitoring job and an alert for CPU usage.3. If you receive an alert, investigate the cause.

1. Change the machine type on the endpoint to have a GPU. Configure the endpoint to enable autoscaling based on the GPU usage.2. Set up a monitoring job and an alert for GPU usage.3. If you receive an alert, investigate the cause.

questions.explanation:
For a Vertex AI endpoint deployment with no accelerators, CPU utilization is the appropriate resource metric for autoscaling replicas. Keeping the machine type sized to the established per-machine QPS and enabling CPU-based autoscaling provides horizontal capacity as traffic rises, while monitoring can surface anomalous resource use for investigation.

**Learn more:** [Scale inference nodes by using autoscaling](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/autoscaling)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a working end-to-end ML pipeline that tunes your ML model’s hyperparameters by using AI Platform, then trains with the best-tuned parameters. Hyperparameter tuning is taking longer than anticipated and is delaying downstream processes. You want to accelerate the tuning job without materially reducing its effectiveness. Which actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Decrease the number of parallel trials.
Decrease the range of floating-point values.
Set the early stopping parameter to TRUE.
Change the search algorithm from Bayesian search to random search.
Decrease the maximum number of trials during subsequent training phases.

questions.explanation:
The goal is to speed up tuning without materially hurting quality. Enabling early stopping (C) terminates unpromising trials before they finish, saving time while still exploring the space, and lowering the maximum number of trials in later phases (E) reduces total work once good regions are found — both cut runtime with minimal loss of effectiveness. Decreasing parallel trials (A) actually lengthens wall-clock time, and switching Bayesian to random search (D) makes the search less sample-efficient, so it would need more trials to reach the same quality. Narrowing the floating-point ranges (B) risks excluding the optimum and materially reducing effectiveness. Thus C and E are the correct pair.

**Learn more:** [Hyperparameter tuning overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/using-hyperparameter-tuning) · [Optimize with Vertex Vizier](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/optimize-your-ml-model-quality-with-vertex-vizier)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You began a classification problem using time-series data and, after only a few experiments, achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC ROC) of 99% on the training data. You have not tried sophisticated algorithms or spent time tuning hyperparameters. What should be your next step to identify and correct the problem?

options.text: Address the model overfitting by using a less complex algorithm.
Address data leakage by applying nested cross-validation during model training.
Address data leakage by removing features highly correlated with the target value.
Address the model overfitting by tuning the hyperparameters to reduce the AUC ROC value.

questions.explanation:
An unexpectedly near-perfect AUC ROC early in a time-series project is a warning sign of data leakage, often caused by validation that permits future information to influence training. Validation for time-series data must preserve temporal order so performance is evaluated on later observations than those used for training. Nested cross-validation provides a validation structure for detecting overly optimistic results and separating evaluation from model-selection activity. scikit-learn documents that ordinary cross-validation can train on future data and evaluate on past data, whereas time-series splits maintain temporal ordering.

**Learn more:** [scikit-learn TimeSeriesSplit documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.TimeSeriesSplit.html) · [scikit-learn cross-validation for time series data](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are the lead ML architect at a small company migrating from on-premises infrastructure to Google Cloud. Your company has limited cloud-infrastructure resources and expertise. You want to begin serving your models from Google Cloud as quickly as possible, using a scalable, reliable, cost-effective solution that needs no additional resources. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Compute Engine VMs to host your models.
Create a Cloud Run function to deploy your models as serverless functions.
Create a managed cluster on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), and deploy your models as containers.
Deploy your models on Vertex AI endpoints.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI endpoints provide managed online model serving in Google Cloud. Models can be deployed to an endpoint for real-time inference, with Google Cloud managing the serving infrastructure and providing deployment autoscaling settings, reducing the operational work required compared with self-managed Compute Engine or GKE deployments.

**Learn more:** [Get online inferences from a custom trained model](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/get-online-predictions) · [gcloud ai endpoints deploy-model](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/endpoints/deploy-model)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for an online publisher that provides news articles to more than 50 million readers. You have built an AI model that recommends content for the company’s weekly newsletter. A recommendation is deemed successful when the article is opened within two days of the newsletter’s publication date and the user stays on the page for at least one minute.  
  
All information required to calculate the success metric is available in BigQuery and updated hourly. The model is trained using eight weeks of data; on average, its performance falls below the acceptable baseline after five weeks; and training takes 12 hours. You want to keep model performance above the acceptable baseline while minimizing cost. How should you monitor the model to determine when retraining is required?

options.text: Use Vertex AI Model Monitoring to detect skew of the input features with a sample rate of 100% and a monitoring frequency of two days.
Schedule a cron job in Cloud Tasks to retrain the model every week before the newsletter is created.
Schedule a weekly query in BigQuery to compute the success metric.
Schedule a daily Dataflow job in Cloud Composer to compute the success metric.

questions.explanation:
The success metric directly measures the model’s required performance outcome, so it should be computed from the BigQuery data after each weekly newsletter cycle. A weekly scheduled BigQuery query provides a timely signal for retraining while avoiding the unnecessary cost of daily processing or fixed weekly retraining. Vertex AI Model Monitoring detects input-feature skew or drift, which is not a direct measurement of this success metric.

**Learn more:** [Model monitoring overview | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/model-monitoring-overview) · [Provide schemas to Vertex AI Model Monitoring | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/model-monitoring/schemas)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You built a custom model in Vertex AI to forecast your company’s product sales from historical transaction data. You expect the feature distributions and correlations among features to change soon. You also anticipate a high volume of prediction requests. You plan to use Vertex AI Model Monitoring for drift detection and want to minimize cost. What should you do?

options.text: Use the features for monitoring. Set a monitoring-frequency value that is higher than the default.
Use the features for monitoring. Set a prediction-sampling-rate value that is closer to 1 than 0.
Use the features and the feature attributions for monitoring. Set a monitoring-frequency value that is lower than the default.
Use the features and the feature attributions for monitoring. Set a prediction-sampling-rate value that is closer to 0 than 1.

questions.explanation:
Feature monitoring identifies changes in input-feature distributions, and feature-attribution monitoring identifies changes in the contribution of features to predictions, helping detect impact from changing feature relationships. A prediction sampling rate closer to 0 logs and analyzes only a subset of the high-volume prediction traffic, reducing Model Monitoring cost while retaining drift detection coverage.

**Learn more:** [Monitor feature attribution skew and drift](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/machine-learning/model-monitoring/monitor-explainable-ai?hl=en) · [Introduction to Model Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/machine-learning/model-monitoring/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a bank. You must train a model using unstructured data in Cloud Storage to predict whether credit card transactions are fraudulent. The data must be converted into a structured format to support analysis in BigQuery. Company policy requires that data containing personally identifiable information (PII) stays in Cloud Storage. You need to implement a scalable solution that retains the data's analytical value. What should you do?

options.text: Use BigQuery’s authorized views and column-level access controls to restrict access to PII within the dataset.
Use the DLP API to de-identify the sensitive data before loading it into BigQuery.
Store the unstructured data in a separate PII-compliant BigQuery database.
Remove the sensitive data from the files manually before loading them into BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Sensitive Data Protection's DLP API can inspect Cloud Storage data for PII and create de-identified copies using transformations such as masking, tokenization, or pseudonymization. The original PII-containing data can remain in Cloud Storage, while the de-identified structured data can be loaded into BigQuery for scalable analysis and model training.

**Learn more:** [Create de-identified copies of data stored in Cloud Storage using the API](https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/deidentify-storage) · [De-identifying sensitive data](https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/deidentify-sensitive-data)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for an ecommerce company that wants to automatically classify products in images to improve the user experience. You have a substantial dataset of labeled images that show various unique products. You need to implement a solution to identify custom products that is scalable, effective, and rapidly deployable. What should you do?

options.text: Develop a rule-based system to categorize the images.
Use a TensorFlow deep learning model that is trained on the image dataset.
Use a pre-trained object detection model from Model Garden.
Use AutoML Vision to train a model using the image dataset.

questions.explanation:
AutoML Vision supports training a custom image-classification model from labeled image data, providing a managed, scalable path to deploy recognition for organization-specific product classes without developing and operating a deep-learning model from scratch. Google Cloud documentation identifies AutoML Vision as a way to train a custom model for targeted image classification.

**Learn more:** [Detect Labels — Cloud Vision API](https://cloud.google.com/vision/docs/labels)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a large social-network service provider where users publish articles and discuss news. Millions of comments are posted online every day, and over 200 human moderators continuously review comments and flag inappropriate ones.  
  
Your team is developing an ML model to assist human moderators in checking platform content. The model scores every comment and flags suspicious comments for human review. Which metric(s) should be used to monitor the model’s performance?

options.text: Number of messages flagged by the model per minute
Number of messages flagged by the model per minute confirmed as being inappropriate by humans.
Precision and recall estimates based on a random sample of 0.1% of raw messages each minute sent to a human for review
Precision and recall estimates based on a sample of messages flagged by the model as potentially inappropriate each minute

questions.explanation:
Precision is the proportion of comments flagged as inappropriate that are truly inappropriate, while recall is the proportion of all truly inappropriate comments that the model flags. Human review of a random sample from the full stream of raw comments provides labels for both model-flagged and model-unflagged comments, allowing both precision and recall to be estimated. A sample restricted to flagged comments omits false negatives, so it cannot measure recall.

**Learn more:** [Classification: Accuracy, recall, precision, and related metrics](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/classification/accuracy-precision-recall)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a model-training pipeline to predict sentiment scores from text-based product reviews. You need control over how the model parameters are tuned, and you will deploy the model to an endpoint once training is complete. You will run the pipeline by using Vertex AI Pipelines. Which Google Cloud pipeline components should you choose?

options.text: TabularDatasetCreateOp, CustomTrainingJobOp, and EndpointCreateOp
TextDatasetCreateOp, AutoMLTextTrainingOp, and EndpointCreateOp
TabularDatasetCreateOp. AutoMLTextTrainingOp, and ModelDeployOp
TextDatasetCreateOp, CustomTrainingJobOp, and ModelDeployOp

questions.explanation:
TextDatasetCreateOp creates a dataset for text-based reviews. CustomTrainingJobOp runs custom model training, allowing control over training configuration and parameter tuning. ModelDeployOp deploys a trained model to a Vertex AI endpoint; creating an endpoint alone does not deploy the model.

**Learn more:** [Vertex AI Pipeline dataset components](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/dataset-component) · [Vertex AI Pipeline CustomJob components](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/customjob-component)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are training a TensorFlow model using a structured dataset containing 100 billion records across several CSV files. You need to improve input/output execution performance. What should you do?

options.text: Load the data into BigQuery, and read the data from BigQuery.
Load the data into Cloud Bigtable, and read the data from Bigtable.
Convert the CSV files into shards of TFRecords, and store the data in Cloud Storage.
Convert the CSV files into shards of TFRecords, and store the data in the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS).

questions.explanation:
TFRecord is TensorFlow’s record-oriented binary format for training input, and sharding data across multiple files enables parallel I/O across hosts. Storing the TFRecord shards in Cloud Storage provides scalable access for the training pipeline.

**Learn more:** [TFRecord and tf.train.Example](https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/load_data/tfrecord) · [Use TPUs](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/tpu)

TensorFlow Serving documents that a single named input can be provided through `instances` using its natural nested tensor shape.

You work for a magazine distributor and must build a model to predict which customers will renew their subscriptions in the coming year. Using your company’s historical data as the training set, you created a TensorFlow model and deployed it to Vertex AI. You need to identify which customer attribute has the greatest predictive power for each prediction the model serves. What should you do?

options.text: Stream prediction results to BigQuery. Use BigQuery’s CORR(X1, X2) function to calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient between each feature and the target variable.
Use Vertex Explainable AI. Submit each prediction request with the explain' keyword to retrieve feature attributions using the sampled Shapley method.
Use Vertex AI Workbench user-managed notebooks to perform a Lasso regression analysis on your model, which will eliminate features that do not provide a strong signal.

Use the What-If tool in Google Cloud to determine how your model will perform when individual features are excluded. Rank the feature importance in order of those that caused the most significant performance drop when removed from the model.

questions.explanation:
Vertex Explainable AI returns feature attributions for individual predictions. For tabular models, sampled Shapley estimates each feature’s contribution to the predicted result, allowing the attribute with the strongest attribution to be identified for each served prediction.

**Learn more:** [Vertex AI Explainable AI overview](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/explainable-ai/overview) · [Get online inferences from a custom-trained model](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/get-online-predictions)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are an ML engineer at a bank. You must build a solution that delivers transparent, understandable explanations for AI-driven decisions involving loan approvals, credit limits, and interest rates. You want the system to have minimal operational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the Learning Interpretability Tool (LIT) on App Engine to provide explainability and visualization of the output.
Use Vertex Explainable AI to generate feature attributions, and use feature-based explanations for your models.
Use AutoML Tables with built-in explainability features, and use Shapley values for explainability.
Deploy pre-trained models from TensorFlow Hub to provide explainability using visualization tools.

questions.explanation:
Vertex Explainable AI is a managed capability that generates feature attributions for model predictions. Feature-based explanations show how individual input features contributed to each decision, supporting transparent explanations for lending outcomes without operating separate explainability infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to Vertex Explainable AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/explainable-ai/overview) · [Explanation — Vertex AI REST reference](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/reference/rest/v1beta1/Explanation)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must build an MLOps pipeline to retrain tree-based models in production. The pipeline will contain components for data ingestion, data processing, model training, model evaluation, and model deployment. Your organization mainly uses PySpark-based workloads for data preprocessing. You want to minimize infrastructure-management effort. How should you configure the pipeline?

options.text: Set up a TensorFlow Extended (TFX) pipeline on Vertex AI Pipelines to orchestrate the MLOps pipeline. Write a custom component for the PySpark-based workloads on Dataproc.
Set up a Vertex AI Pipelines to orchestrate the MLOps pipeline. Use the predefined Dataproc component for the PySpark-based workloads.
Set up Kubeflow Pipelines on Google Kubernetes Engine to orchestrate the MLOps pipeline. Write a custom component for the PySparkbased workloads on Dataproc.
Set up Cloud Composer to orchestrate the MLOps pipeline. Use Dataproc workflow templates for the PySpark-based workloads in Cloud Composer.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Pipelines provides serverless ML pipeline orchestration, and its predefined Serverless for Apache Spark components include `DataprocPySparkBatchOp` for PySpark batch workloads. Serverless for Apache Spark runs the batch workload on managed, automatically scaling compute, avoiding the operational burden of managing a GKE-based Kubeflow installation or custom orchestration components.

**Learn more:** [Vertex AI Pipelines overview](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/introduction) · [Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark components](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/dataproc-component)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You developed a BigQuery ML model that predicts customer chum and deployed it to Vertex AI Endpoints. You want to automate retraining when model feature values change while using minimal additional code. You also want to minimize how often the model is retrained to reduce training costs. What should you do?

options.text: 1 Enable request-response logging on Vertex AI Endpoints2. Schedule a TensorFlow Data Validation job to monitor prediction drift3. Execute model retraining if there is significant distance between the distributions

1. Enable request-response logging on Vertex AI Endpoints2. Schedule a TensorFlow Data Validation job to monitor training/serving skew3. Execute model retraining if there is significant distance between the distributions

1. Create a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job configured to monitor prediction drift2. Configure alert monitoring to publish a message to a Pub/Sub queue when a monitoring alert is detected3. Use a Cloud Function to monitor the Pub/Sub queue, and trigger retraining in BigQuery

1. Create a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job configured to monitor training/serving skew2. Configure alert monitoring to publish a message to a Pub/Sub queue when a monitoring alert is detected3. Use a Cloud Function to monitor the Pub/Sub queue, and trigger retraining in BigQuery

questions.explanation:
Training-serving skew is a significant difference between feature-value distributions in the training data and in production serving requests. Vertex AI Model Monitoring can detect that skew against a training baseline and emit anomaly notifications when configured thresholds are exceeded. Sending those notifications to Pub/Sub and triggering BigQuery retraining with a Cloud Function makes retraining conditional on meaningful feature-distribution changes, avoiding unnecessary retraining costs.

**Learn more:** [Provide schemas to Vertex AI Model Monitoring](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/model-monitoring/schemas) · [ModelMonitoringNotificationSpec](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/reference/rest/v1beta1/ModelMonitoringNotificationSpec)

You deployed a scikit-learn model to a Vertex AI endpoint through a custom model server. You enabled autoscaling; however, the deployed model does not scale beyond one replica, resulting in dropped requests. CPU utilization stays low even during high-load periods. What should you do?

options.text: Attach a GPU to the prediction nodes
Increase the number of workers in your model server
Schedule scaling of the nodes to match expected demand
Increase the minReplicaCount in your DeployedModel configuration

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI can scale a deployment according to per-replica CPU utilization. A custom model server with too few workers may handle requests serially and leave much of a multi-core prediction node idle, so the CPU-based autoscaler does not reach its target even while requests are being dropped. Increasing the number of model-server workers enables concurrent inference processing, better uses the available CPU, and lets CPU-based autoscaling respond to demand. [Scale inference nodes using autoscaling | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/autoscaling)

**Learn more:** [Scale inference nodes using autoscaling | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/autoscaling)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently trained an XGBoost model that you intend to deploy to production for online inference. Before you send a prediction request to the model binary, you must perform a simple data-preprocessing step. This step exposes a REST API that accepts requests within your internal VPC Service Controls and returns predictions. You want to configure this preprocessing step while minimizing cost and effort. What should you do?

options.text: Store a pickled model in Cloud Storage. Build a Flask-based app, package the app in a custom container image, and deploy the model to Vertex AI Endpoints.
Build a Flask-based app, package the app and a pickled model in a custom container image, and deploy the model to Vertex AI Endpoints.

Build a custom predictor class based on XGBoost Predictor from the Vertex AI SDK, package it and a pickled model in a custom container image based on a Vertex built-in image, and deploy the model to Vertex AI Endpoints.

Build a custom predictor class based on XGBoost Predictor from the Vertex AI SDK, and package the handler in a custom container image based on a Vertex built-in container image. Store a pickled model in Cloud Storage, and deploy the model to Vertex AI Endpoints.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Custom Prediction Routines allow preprocessing logic to run as part of an online prediction request. A custom predictor derived from the SDK’s XGBoost predictor can implement that preprocessing while reusing the framework’s model-loading and prediction behavior. The serialized model belongs in Cloud Storage as the model artifact, and Vertex AI supplies the serving infrastructure, avoiding the effort of implementing and operating a separate Flask server or baking the model into the container image.

**Learn more:** [Custom prediction routines | Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/custom-prediction-routines) · [Predictor class | Vertex AI SDK for Python](https://cloud.google.com/python/docs/reference/aiplatform/latest/google.cloud.aiplatform.prediction.Predictor)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a company that constructs bridges for cities worldwide. To monitor project progress at construction sites, the company has installed cameras at every location. Each hour, the cameras capture a picture and send it to a Cloud Storage bucket. A team of specialists reviews the images, filters the important ones, and annotates particular objects within them. You want to recommend an ML solution that helps the company scale while reducing costs. The solution must have minimal up-front cost. What method should you recommend?

options.text: Train an AutoML object detection model to annotate the objects in the images to help specialists with the annotation task.
Use the Cloud Vision API to automatically annotate objects in the images to help specialists with the annotation task.
Create a BigQuery ML classification model to classify important images. Use the model to predict which new images are important to help specialists with the filtering task.
Use Vertex AI to train an open source object detection to annotate the objects in the images to help specialists with the annotation task.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Vision API provides pre-trained image-analysis capabilities, including object localization and labels, so it can automatically annotate common objects and assist the specialists without building and training a custom model. It is pay-as-you-go with no up-front commitment, making it the lowest up-front-cost option.

**Learn more:** [Detect multiple objects | Cloud Vision API](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vision/docs/object-localizer) · [Cloud Vision API pricing](https://cloud.google.com/vision/pricing)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You trained a deep neural network model on Google Cloud. It has low loss on the training data but performs worse on the validation data. You want the model to be robust against overfitting. Which strategy should you use when retraining the model?

options.text: Apply a dropout parameter of 0.2, and decrease the learning rate by a factor of 10.
Apply a L2 regularization parameter of 0.4, and decrease the learning rate by a factor of 10.
Run a hyperparameter tuning job on AI Platform to optimize for the L2 regularization and dropout parameters.
Run a hyperparameter tuning job on AI Platform to optimize for the learning rate, and increase the number of neurons by a factor of 2.

questions.explanation:
Overfitting is indicated by substantially better training performance than validation performance. L2 regularization penalizes overly large weights, and dropout reduces co-adaptation among neurons; tuning both against a validation metric selects suitable regularization strength for the specific model and data. Google Cloud hyperparameter tuning jobs search for optimal combinations of specified hyperparameters across trials.

**Learn more:** [Create a hyperparameter tuning job](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/using-hyperparameter-tuning)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to build an ML model for a social media application that predicts whether a user-submitted profile photo meets the requirements. The application will tell the user whether the picture meets those requirements. How should you build a model to ensure that the application does not incorrectly accept a non-compliant picture?

options.text: Use AutoML to optimize the model’s recall in order to minimize false negatives.
Use AutoML to optimize the model’s F1 score in order to balance the accuracy of false positives and false negatives.
Use Vertex AI Workbench user-managed notebooks to build a custom model that has three times as many examples of pictures that meet the profile photo requirements.
Use Vertex AI Workbench user-managed notebooks to build a custom model that has three times as many examples of pictures that do not meet the profile photo requirements.

questions.explanation:
A non-compliant picture that is predicted as meeting the requirements is a false positive for the accepted/compliant class. Training with three times as many non-compliant examples places greater emphasis on recognizing the rejection class, helping reduce such false acceptances. Recall focuses on false negatives, while F1 gives precision and recall equal consideration rather than specifically prioritizing false-positive reduction.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to tabular data](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/tabular101)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are on the data science team at a manufacturing company.
