For exploratory data analysis, you must calculate descriptive statistics, such as mean, median, and mode; perform complex statistical tests for hypothesis testing; and plot feature variation over time. You want to use as much of the sales data as possible in the analyses while minimizing computational resources. What should you do?

options.text: Visualize the time plots in Google Data Studio. Import the dataset into Vertex Al Workbench user-managed notebooks. Use this data to calculate the descriptive statistics and run the statistical analyses.
Spin up a Vertex Al Workbench user-managed notebooks instance and import the dataset. Use this data to create statistical and visual analyses.
Use BigQuery to calculate the descriptive statistics. Use Vertex Al Workbench user-managed notebooks to visualize the time plots and run the statistical analyses.
Use BigQuery to calculate the descriptive statistics, and use Google Data Studio to visualize the time plots. Use Vertex Al Workbench user-managed notebooks to run the statistical analyses.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery can execute aggregate and statistical calculations across very large datasets without loading all records into notebook memory. Looker Studio supports time-series charts for displaying how metrics change over time. Vertex AI Workbench notebooks provide an interactive programming environment for complex statistical hypothesis testing, so reserving them for that work minimizes compute and data movement.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery aggregate functions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/aggregate_functions) · [Types of charts in Looker Studio](https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/studio/types-of-charts-in-looker-studio)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team must create a Google Cloud ML solution that classifies support requests for one of your platforms. After analyzing the requirements, you chose TensorFlow for the classifier to retain full control over the model code, serving, and deployment. You will use Kubeflow pipelines as the ML platform. To reduce development time, you want to build on existing resources and use managed services rather than create an entirely new model. How should you build the classifier?

options.text: Use the Natural Language API to classify support requests.
Use AutoML Natural Language to build the support requests classifier.
Use an established text classification model on AI Platform to perform transfer learning.
Use an established text classification model on AI Platform as-is to classify support requests.

questions.explanation:
Transfer learning adapts an established pre-trained text model to the organization’s support-request categories, reducing training effort while preserving control of TensorFlow model code and its serving and deployment. TensorFlow Hub supports text classification using pre-trained text embeddings and transfer learning, and Google Cloud’s managed ML platform supports custom training and deployment with TensorFlow.

**Learn more:** [Text classification with TensorFlow Hub: Movie reviews](https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/keras/text_classification_with_hub) · [Introduction to Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/ai-platform/docs/technical-overview)

questions.question: You are working on a neural network-based project. The dataset supplied to you contains columns with differing ranges. While preparing data for model training, you find that gradient optimization is struggling to move the weights toward a good solution. What should you do?

options.text: Use feature construction to combine the strongest features.
Use the representation transformation (normalization) technique.
Improve the data cleaning step by removing features with missing values.
Change the partitioning step to reduce the dimension of the test set and have a larger training set.

questions.explanation: Feature normalization transforms input columns to comparable ranges or distributions, improving the conditioning of gradient-based neural-network training and allowing weight updates to converge more effectively.

questions.question: You are working on a neural network-based project. The dataset supplied to you contains columns with differing ranges. While preparing data for model training, you find that gradient optimization is struggling to move the weights toward a good solution. What should you do?

options.text: Create a custom TensorFlow DNN model
Use BQML XGBoost regression to train the model.
Use AutoML Tables to train the model without early stopping.
Use AutoML Tables to train the model with RMSLE as the optimization objective.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML boosted-tree regression is powered by XGBoost and trains directly against BigQuery data, avoiding custom TensorFlow development and data movement. Gradient-boosted trees are well suited to mixed tabular features and regression targets that can be negative. RMSLE is not appropriate for negative targets, and turning off early stopping can increase AutoML training time without matching the stated efficiency goal.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery ML CREATE MODEL statement for boosted trees using XGBoost](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/bigqueryml-syntax-create-boosted-tree)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to train a computer-vision model that predicts the government ID type shown in a given image, using a GPU-powered virtual machine on Compute Engine. You use these parameters:  
  
- Optimizer: SGD  
- Image shape = 224×224  
- Batch size = 64  
- Epochs = 10  
- Verbose = 2  
  
While training, you encounter this error: `ResourceExhaustedError: Out Of Memory (OOM) when allocating tensor`. What should you do?

options.text: Change the optimizer.
Reduce the batch size.
Change the learning rate.
Reduce the image shape.

questions.explanation:
An out-of-memory `ResourceExhaustedError` occurs when the tensors required for a training step exceed available GPU memory. A smaller batch keeps fewer images and their intermediate activations and gradients in memory at once, reducing the allocation requirement. TensorFlow specifically recommends using a smaller batch size for OOM-related `ResourceExhaustedError` failures.

**Learn more:** [tf.errors.ResourceExhaustedError | TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/errors/ResourceExhaustedError)

options.text: Export the model to BigQuery ML.
Deploy and version the model on AI Platform.
Use Dataflow with the SavedModel to read the data from BigQuery.
Submit a batch prediction job on AI Platform that points to the model location in Cloud Storage.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML supports importing a TensorFlow SavedModel from Cloud Storage and running `ML.PREDICT` directly on data in BigQuery. This keeps inference close to the BigQuery data and avoids the additional deployment or data-processing overhead of AI Platform batch prediction or Dataflow.

**Learn more:** [Make predictions with imported TensorFlow models](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/making-predictions-with-imported-tensorflow-models) · [CREATE MODEL statement for importing TensorFlow models](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/bigqueryml-syntax-create-tensorflow)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently deployed a scikit-learn model to a Vertex AI endpoint and are testing it with live production traffic. While monitoring the endpoint, you find that it receives twice as many requests per hour as expected throughout the day. You want the endpoint to scale efficiently when demand grows in the future so that users do not experience high latency. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy two models to the same endpoint, and distribute requests among them evenly
Configure an appropriate minReplicaCount value based on expected baseline traffic
Set the target utilization percentage in the autoscailngMetricSpecs configuration to a higher value
Change the model’s machine type to one that utilizes GPUs

questions.explanation:
For Vertex AI online prediction, `minReplicaCount` defines the minimum number of machine replicas kept deployed. Setting it to match the newly observed baseline traffic provides sufficient always-available capacity, while Vertex AI can add replicas as traffic increases. A higher utilization target delays scale-out and can increase latency under load.

**Learn more:** [DedicatedResources | Vertex AI](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/reference/rest/v1/DedicatedResources)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You developed a custom ML model with scikit-learn. Its training time is longer than anticipated. You decide to move the model to Vertex AI Training and want to reduce its training time. What should you try first?

options.text: Train your model in a distributed mode using multiple Compute Engine VMs.
Train your model using Vertex AI Training with CPUs.
Migrate your model to TensorFlow, and train it using Vertex AI Training.
Train your model using Vertex AI Training with GPUs.

questions.explanation:
Existing scikit-learn training code is generally CPU-based, so Vertex AI Training with CPUs is the appropriate first migration path. GPUs improve training only when the framework and training code can use them; Vertex AI notes that some ML frameworks cannot use GPUs, and scikit-learn support is limited to certain experimental Array API-compatible estimators. Distributed execution or rewriting the model in TensorFlow introduces additional implementation work before establishing a baseline.

**Learn more:** [Prepare training code — Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/code-requirements) · [Frequently Asked Questions — scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/faq.html)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are training an ML model with data stored in BigQuery that includes several values considered Personally Identifiable Information (PII). You must reduce the dataset’s sensitivity before training the model. Every column is essential to the model. How should you proceed?

options.text: Using Dataflow, ingest the columns with sensitive data from BigQuery, and then randomize the values in each sensitive column.
Use the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP) API to scan for sensitive data, and use Dataflow with the DLP API to encrypt sensitive values with Format Preserving Encryption.
Use the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP) API to scan for sensitive data, and use Dataflow to replace all sensitive data by using the encryption algorithm AES-256 with a salt.

Before training, use BigQuery to select only the columns that do not contain sensitive data. Create an authorized view of the data so that sensitive values cannot be accessed by unauthorized individuals.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Sensitive Data Protection can scan BigQuery data for PII and de-identify it through format-preserving encryption. Format-preserving encryption replaces sensitive values with encrypted tokens while preserving their character set and length, allowing every required column to remain available for model training with reduced exposure of the original PII.

**Learn more:** [Transformation reference — Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/transformations-reference?hl=en) · [Using Sensitive Data Protection with BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/dlp-bigquery)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a large collection of written support cases that fall into 3 distinct categories: Technical Support, Billing Support, or Other Issues. You need to rapidly build, test, and deploy a service that automatically assigns future written requests to one of these categories. How should you configure the pipeline?

options.text: Use the Cloud Natural Language API to obtain metadata to classify the incoming cases.
Use AutoML Natural Language to build and test a classifier. Deploy the model as a REST API.
Use BigQuery ML to build and test a logistic regression model to classify incoming requests. Use BigQuery ML to perform inference.
Create a TensorFlow model using Google’s BERT pre-trained model. Build and test a classifier, and deploy the model using Vertex AI.

questions.explanation:
AutoML Natural Language supports supervised text classification using labeled examples, including evaluation of the trained classifier and online prediction through a REST API. It best fits a rapid managed workflow for assigning each incoming support request to one mutually exclusive category.

**Learn more:** [Vertex AI: Predict for text classification single label](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/samples/aiplatform-predict-text-classification-single-label-sample?hl=en) · [Vertex AI: Evaluate AutoML text-classification models](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/text-data/classification/evaluate-model)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a data science team at a large international corporation. Most models the team trains are large-scale models that use high-level TensorFlow APIs on AI Platform with GPUs. The team typically spends a few weeks or months iterating on a new model version. You have recently been asked to review the team’s spending.  
  
How should you lower Google Cloud compute costs without affecting model performance?

options.text: Use AI Platform to run distributed training jobs with checkpoints.
Use AI Platform to run distributed training jobs without checkpoints.
Migrate to training with Kuberflow on Google Kubernetes Engine, and use preemptible VMs with checkpoints.
Migrate to training with Kuberflow on Google Kubernetes Engine, and use preemptible VMs without checkpoints.

questions.explanation:
Preemptible VMs offer lower-cost compute but can be terminated. A long-running training workload can retain its results and resume after an interruption by writing periodic checkpoints, making fault-tolerant Kubeflow training on GKE preemptible VMs an appropriate cost-saving approach without sacrificing the model’s training outcome.

**Learn more:** [Run fault-tolerant workloads at lower costs with Spot VMs](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/spot-vms) · [Spot VMs](https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/spot-vms)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are working with a dataset that includes customer transactions. You need to build an ML model that predicts customer purchase behavior. You intend to develop the model in BigQuery ML and export it to Cloud Storage for online prediction. The input data includes a few categorical features, including product category and payment method. You want to deploy the model as fast as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Use the TRANSFORM clause with the ML.ONE_HOT_ENCODER function on the categorical features at model creation and select the categorical and non-categorical features.
Use the ML.ONE_HOT_ENCODER function on the categorical features and select the encoded categorical features and non-categorical features as inputs to create your model.
Use the CREATE MODEL statement and select the categorical and non-categorical features.
Use the ML.MULTI_HOT_ENCODER function on the categorical features, and select the encoded categorical features and non-categorical features as inputs to create your model.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML automatically preprocesses categorical feature columns during `CREATE MODEL`; non-array categorical values are automatically encoded as appropriate. Its automatic preprocessing is preserved in exported model artifacts, so no explicit one-hot or multi-hot feature engineering is needed before online prediction.

**Learn more:** [Automatic feature preprocessing | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/auto-preprocessing?hl=en) · [Export models | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/exporting-models?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a retail company and have created a Vertex AI forecast model that generates monthly predictions of item sales. You need to quickly create a report that helps explain how the model calculates its predictions. You have one month of recent actual sales data that was not included in the training dataset. How should you generate the data for the report?

options.text: Create a batch prediction job by using the actual sales data. Compare the predictions to the actuals in the report.
Create a batch prediction job by using the actual sales data, and configure the job settings to generate feature attributions. Compare the results in the report.
Generate counterfactual examples by using the actual sales data. Create a batch prediction job using the actual sales data and the counterfactual examples. Compare the results in the report.

Train another model by using the same training dataset as the original, and exclude some columns. Using the actual sales data create one batch prediction job by using the new model and another one with the original model. Compare the two sets of predictions in the report.

questions.explanation:
Feature attributions provide local explanations by showing how much each input feature contributed to an individual forecast prediction. Enabling feature attributions in a batch prediction job produces explanation data together with the predictions, allowing those predictions to be compared with the held-out actual sales in the report.

**Learn more:** [Get batch inferences for a forecast model](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/tabular-workflows/forecasting-batch-predictions) · [Feature attributions for forecasting](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/tabular-workflows/forecasting-feature-attribution)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are investigating the root cause of a misclassification made by one of your models. You used Vertex AI Pipelines to train and deploy the model. The pipeline reads data from BigQuery, creates a copy of the data in Cloud Storage in TFRecord format, trains the model in Vertex AI Training using that copy, and deploys the model to a Vertex AI endpoint. You have identified the particular version of the model that misclassified, and need to recover the data on which this model was trained. How should you locate that data copy?

options.text: Use Vertex AI Feature Store. Modify the pipeline to use the feature store, and ensure that all training data is stored in it. Search the feature store for the data used for the training.

Use the lineage feature of Vertex AI Metadata to find the model artifact. Determine the version of the model and identify the step that creates the data copy and search in the metadata for its location.

Use the logging features in the Vertex AI endpoint to determine the timestamp of the model’s deployment. Find the pipeline run at that timestamp. Identify the step that creates the data copy, and search in the logs for its location.
Find the job ID in Vertex AI Training corresponding to the training for the model. Search in the logs of that job for the data used for the training.

questions.explanation:
Vertex ML Metadata stores the artifacts and executions for Vertex AI Pipeline runs and supports lineage analysis. The lineage of a model can include the training data used to create it. Tracing the identified model artifact backward to the pipeline execution that produced the TFRecord artifact reveals that artifact’s Cloud Storage URI, which identifies the exact data copy used for training.

**Learn more:** [Track the lineage of pipeline artifacts](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/lineage) · [Visualize and analyze pipeline results](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/visualize-pipeline)

options.text: Implement continuous retraining of the model daily using Vertex AI Pipelines.
Add a model monitoring job where 10% of incoming predictions are sampled 24 hours.
Add a model monitoring job where 90% of incoming predictions are sampled 24 hours.
Add a model monitoring job where 10% of incoming predictions are sampled every hour.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Model Monitoring detects feature drift by analyzing sampled production inference inputs against a baseline feature distribution. Monitoring a cost-efficient subset of requests at an hourly frequency provides timely detection of substantial production-distribution changes; automatic daily retraining does not itself detect drift.

**Learn more:** [gcloud ai model-monitoring-jobs create](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/model-monitoring-jobs/create) · [Vertex AI Model Monitoring capabilities](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/get-to-know-vertex-ai-model-monitoring)

You recently deployed a model to a Vertex AI endpoint. Because your data drifts frequently, you enabled request-response logging and created a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job. You have found that the model receives more traffic than expected. You need to lower model-monitoring cost while still detecting drift quickly. What should you do?

options.text: Replace the monitoring job with a DataFlow pipeline that uses TensorFlow Data Validation (TFDV)
Replace the monitoring job with a custom SQL script to calculate statistics on the features and predictions in BigQuery
Decrease the sample_rate parameter in the RandomSampleConfig of the monitoring job
Increase the monitor_interval parameter in the ScheduleConfig of the monitoring job

questions.explanation:
The prediction sampling rate controls the proportion of endpoint prediction requests collected for monitoring. Decreasing it reduces the logged and analyzed request volume—and therefore monitoring cost—while preserving the monitoring schedule so drift can still be detected promptly.

**Learn more:** [gcloud ai model-monitoring-jobs update](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/model-monitoring-jobs/update)

questions.explanation:

You have been tasked with ensuring that ML models are developed securely. In particular, you must protect sensitive customer data that might be used in the models. options.text: Tokenize all of the fields using hashed dummy values to replace the real values.
Use principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce the four sensitive fields to one PCA vector.
Coarsen the data by putting AGE into quantiles and rounding LATITUDE_LONGTTUDE into single precision. The other two fields are already as coarse as possible.
Remove all sensitive data fields, and ask the data science team to build their models using non-sensitive data.

questions.explanation:
Data minimization and generalization reduce exposure of sensitive attributes while preserving useful training features. Binning age into quantiles and lowering location precision reduce identifiability; a Boolean existing-customer indicator and categorical shirt size are already coarse representations. AWS guidance recommends applying data-minimization and privacy-preserving transformations to sensitive ML training data while maintaining model utility.

AWS guidance recommends applying data-minimization and privacy-preserving transformations to sensitive ML training data while maintaining model utility.

**Learn more:** [AWS Machine Learning Lens — Protect sensitive data privacy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/machine-learning-lens/mlsec03-bp03.html) · [AWS Machine Learning Lens — Keep only relevant data](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/machine-learning-lens/mlsec03-bp05.html)","trackingInfo":{"questionId":"e44f82e4-23c8-4a76-abd3-753f236e367c","examProvider":"google","examName":"professional-machine-learning-engineer","mode":"default"}}]]
You manage a team of data scientists who use a cloud-based backend to submit training jobs. The system has become very difficult to administer, and you want to move to a managed service. The data scientists use many different frameworks, including Keras, PyTorch, theano, Scikit-learn, and custom libraries. What should you do?

options.text: Use the AI Platform custom containers feature to receive training jobs using any framework.
Configure Kubeflow to run on Google Kubernetes Engine and receive training jobs through TF Job.
Create a library of VM images on Compute Engine, and publish these images on a centralized repository.
Set up Slurm workload manager to receive jobs that can be scheduled to run on your cloud infrastructure.

questions.explanation:
Custom training containers package the training application together with its chosen ML framework, dependencies, libraries, and binaries. This enables a managed AI Platform/Vertex AI training service to run jobs using frameworks not covered by prebuilt containers, including custom libraries, without operating the underlying training platform.

**Learn more:** [Vertex AI custom containers overview](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/containers-overview)

You developed a BigQuery ML linear-regression model using a training dataset stored in a BigQuery table. New data is added to the table every minute. You use Cloud Scheduler and Vertex AI Pipelines to automate hourly model training, and you use the model for direct inference. The feature-preprocessing logic includes quantile bucketization and MinMax scaling on data received in the last hour. You want to minimize storage and computational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Preprocess and stage the data in BigQuery prior to feeding it to the model during training and inference.
Use the TRANSFORM clause in the CREATE MODEL statement in the SQL query to calculate the required statistics.
Create a component in the Vertex AI Pipelines directed acyclic graph (DAG) to calculate the required statistics, and pass the statistics on to subsequent components.
Create SQL queries to calculate and store the required statistics in separate BigQuery tables that are referenced in the CREATE MODEL statement.

questions.explanation:
A `TRANSFORM` clause in a BigQuery ML `CREATE MODEL` statement can apply `ML.QUANTILE_BUCKETIZE` and `ML.MIN_MAX_SCALER`. BigQuery ML calculates the required training statistics and stores them with the model; it automatically reuses those statistics when transforming inference inputs. This provides consistent training and prediction preprocessing without staging transformed data or maintaining separate statistics tables or pipeline components.

**Learn more:** [Manual feature preprocessing | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/manual-preprocessing) · [The CREATE MODEL statement | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/bigqueryml-syntax-create)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You created a custom model with Vertex AI to predict the user churn rate for your application. You use Vertex AI Model Monitoring for skew detection. The training data in BigQuery contains two feature sets: demographic and behavioral. You later find that two separate models, each trained on one feature set, perform better than the original model. You need to configure a new model-monitoring pipeline that distributes traffic between the two models. You want to use the same prediction-sampling-rate and monitoring-frequency for each model, while minimizing management effort. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the training dataset as is. Deploy the models to two separate endpoints, and submit two Vertex AI Model Monitoring jobs with appropriately selected feature-thresholds parameters.

Keep the training dataset as is. Deploy both models to the same endpoint and submit a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job with a monitoring-config-from-file parameter that accounts for the model IDs and feature selections.
Separate the training dataset into two tables based on demographic and behavioral features. Deploy the models to two separate endpoints, and submit two Vertex AI Model Monitoring jobs.

Separate the training dataset into two tables based on demographic and behavioral features. Deploy both models to the same endpoint, and submit a Vertex AI Model Monitoring job with a monitoring-config-from-file parameter that accounts for the model IDs and training datasets.

questions.explanation:
Training-serving skew detection requires the training dataset baseline to match the features used by the monitored model. Separate the demographic and behavioral training data into distinct tables, deploy both models to one endpoint for traffic splitting, and create one monitoring job. Its configuration file can define a separate monitoring objective for each deployed model, including that model’s training dataset, while the monitoring job shares one prediction sampling rate and monitoring frequency.

**Learn more:** [gcloud alpha ai model-monitoring-jobs create](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/alpha/ai/model-monitoring-jobs/create) · [gcloud ai model-monitoring-jobs update](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/model-monitoring-jobs/update)

You work for a retail company and have a managed tabular dataset in Vertex AI containing sales data from three different stores. The dataset includes several features, including store name and sale timestamp. You want to use this data to train a model that predicts sales for a new store that will open soon. You must split the data into training, validation, and test sets. Which approach should you use to split the data?

options.text: Use Vertex AI manual split, using the store name feature to assign one store for each set
Use Vertex AI default data split
Use Vertex AI chronological split, and specify the sales timestamp feature as the time variable
Use Vertex AI random split, assigning 70% of the rows to the training set, 10% to the validation set, and 20% to the test set

questions.explanation:
To assess performance for a store not represented during training, split the dataset by store so that each store’s rows are isolated in a single dataset split. This prevents store-specific information from appearing in both training and evaluation data and tests generalization to an unseen store. Vertex AI documentation specifically recommends splitting purchase data by store when predictions will be made primarily for stores not present in the training data.

**Learn more:** [Data splits for tabular data](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/data-splits)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are solving a classification problem using time-series data. After performing only a few experiments with random cross-validation, you obtained an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC ROC) of 99% on the training data. You have not tried sophisticated algorithms or spent time tuning hyperparameters. What should be your next step to identify and correct the problem?

options.text: Address the model overfitting by using a less complex algorithm and use k-fold cross-validation.
Address data leakage by applying nested cross-validation during model training.
Address data leakage by removing features highly correlated with the target value.
Address the model overfitting by tuning the hyperparameters to reduce the AUC ROC value.

questions.explanation:
An unexpectedly near-perfect AUC from simple experiments is a strong indicator that a feature may expose the target directly or indirectly. Features that are highly correlated with the target should be investigated and removed when they contain information unavailable at prediction time, because such leakage produces overly optimistic validation results. Random cross-validation can also inflate estimates for time-series data by mixing temporally related observations across splits.

**Learn more:** [scikit-learn: Common pitfalls and recommended practices](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html) · [scikit-learn: Cross-validation of time series data](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are an ML engineer at a manufacturing company developing a classification model for a predictive-maintenance use case. You must predict whether a critical machine will fail within the next three days, giving the repair crew enough time to fix it before it breaks. Regular machine maintenance is relatively inexpensive, but a failure would be very costly. You have trained several binary classifiers to predict whether the machine will fail; a prediction of 1 means the ML model predicts a failure.  
  
You are now evaluating each model on an evaluation dataset. You want to select a model that prioritizes detection while ensuring that more than 50% of the maintenance jobs initiated by the model address an imminent machine failure. Which model should you choose?

options.text: The model with the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC ROC) and precision greater than 0.5
The model with the lowest root mean squared error (RMSE) and recall greater than 0.5.
The model with the highest recall where precision is greater than 0.5.
The model with the highest precision where recall is greater than 0.5.

questions.explanation:
Recall measures the proportion of actual imminent machine failures that are detected, so maximizing recall prioritizes detection and reduces costly missed failures. Precision measures the proportion of maintenance-triggering failure predictions that are correct; requiring precision greater than 0.5 ensures that more than half of triggered maintenance jobs address real imminent failures. This is the recall-at-precision objective described in Vertex AI documentation.

**Learn more:** [Train a model with End-to-End AutoML](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/tabular-workflows/e2e-automl-train) · [Introduction to tabular data](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/tabular101)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are creating an ML pipeline to process and analyze both streaming and batch datasets. The pipeline must handle data validation, preprocessing, model training, and model deployment consistently and automatically. You want an efficient, scalable solution that records model-training metadata and is easy to reproduce. You also want to reuse custom components across different parts of the pipeline. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Composer for distributed processing of batch and streaming data in the pipeline.
Use Dataflow for distributed processing of batch and streaming data in the pipeline.
Use Cloud Build to build and push Docker images for each pipeline component.
Implement an orchestration framework such as Kubeflow Pipelines or Vertex AI Pipelines.

questions.explanation:
Kubeflow Pipelines and Vertex AI Pipelines provide end-to-end ML workflow orchestration with reusable components, automated execution, and tracking of pipeline artifacts and metadata. Vertex AI Pipelines integrates with Vertex ML Metadata for lineage, execution tracking, and reproducibility, while its components can invoke services such as Dataflow when distributed batch or streaming processing is needed.

**Learn more:** [Architecture for MLOps using TensorFlow Extended, Vertex AI Pipelines, and Cloud Build](https://cloud.google.com/solutions/machine-learning/architecture-for-mlops-using-tfx-kubeflow-pipelines-and-cloud-build) · [Visualize and analyze pipeline results](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/visualize-pipeline)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are a SQL analyst. You need to use a TensorFlow customer-segmentation model stored in Cloud Storage. You want the simplest and most efficient approach. What should you do?

options.text: Import the model into Vertex AI Model Registry. Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint, and use SQL for inference in BigQuery.
Deploy the model by using TensorFlow Serving, and call for inference from BigQuery.
Convert the model into a BigQuery ML model, and use SQL for inference.
Import the model into BigQuery, and use SQL for inference.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML can import a TensorFlow SavedModel from Cloud Storage as a BigQuery ML model and run inference using GoogleSQL with `ML.PREDICT`. This is a fully managed SQL-based approach and avoids endpoint deployment or managing TensorFlow Serving.

**Learn more:** [The CREATE MODEL statement for importing TensorFlow models](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/bigqueryml-syntax-create-tensorflow) · [Make predictions with imported TensorFlow models](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/making-predictions-with-imported-tensorflow-models)

You are developing a prototype text-classification model in a managed Vertex AI Workbench notebook. You want to quickly experiment with tokenizing text using the Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK) library. How should you add the library to your Jupyter kernel?

options.text: Install the NLTK library from a terminal by using the pip install nltk command.
Write a custom Dataflow job that uses NLTK to tokenize your text and saves the output to Cloud Storage.
Create a new Vertex AI Workbench notebook with a custom image that includes the NLTK library.
Install the NLTK library from a Jupyter cell by using the !pip install nltk --user command.

questions.explanation:
A Jupyter notebook cell can invoke pip with `!pip install nltk --user` to install NLTK for the notebook user and make it available to the kernel after a kernel restart if required. The `--user` option installs the package in the user directory, which Vertex AI Workbench preserves across upgrades.

**Learn more:** [Use Private Service Connect to access a Vector Search index from an on-premises environment](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/general/vertex-psc-vector-search) · [Upgrade the environment of a Vertex AI Workbench instance](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/workbench/instances/upgrade)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You want to train an AutoML model to predict home prices using a small public dataset stored in BigQuery. You need to prepare the data and want the simplest, most efficient approach. What should you do?

options.text: Write a query that preprocesses the data by using BigQuery and creates a new table. Create a Vertex AI managed dataset with the new table as the data source.
Use Dataflow to preprocess the data. Write the output in TFRecord format to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Write a query that preprocesses the data by using BigQuery. Export the query results as CSV files, and use those files to create a Vertex AI managed dataset.
Use a Vertex AI Workbench notebook instance to preprocess the data by using the pandas library. Export the data as CSV files, and use those files to create a Vertex AI managed dataset.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI tabular AutoML supports BigQuery tables as training-data sources. Preprocessing directly in BigQuery and storing the result in a new BigQuery table keeps the data in its existing analytics service and avoids unnecessary pipeline infrastructure, notebook processing, or CSV/TFRecord exports. [Vertex AI managed datasets documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/using-managed-datasets)

**Learn more:** [Use managed datasets](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/using-managed-datasets) · [Create a Vertex AI tabular dataset](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tutorials/tabular-bq-prediction/create-dataset)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a bank and have been asked to develop an ML model to support loan-application decisions. You need to determine which Vertex AI services to include in the workflow. You want to track the model's training parameters and metrics for each training epoch. You plan to compare the performance of every model version to identify the best model using your selected metrics. Which Vertex AI services should you use?

options.text: Vertex ML Metadata, Vertex AI Feature Store, and Vertex AI Vizier
Vertex AI Pipelines, Vertex AI Experiments, and Vertex AI Vizier
Vertex ML Metadata, Vertex AI Experiments, and Vertex AI TensorBoard
Vertex AI Pipelines, Vertex AI Feature Store, and Vertex AI TensorBoard

questions.explanation:
Vertex ML Metadata tracks ML artifacts, parameters, and metrics. Vertex AI Experiments organizes experiment runs and supports comparing their parameters and metrics across model versions. Vertex AI TensorBoard stores and visualizes time-series training metrics, including metrics recorded for each epoch.

**Learn more:** [Vertex ML Metadata notebook tutorials](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/ml-metadata/ml-metadata-notebook-tutorials) · [Configure your training script](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/experiments/configure-training-script)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],One of your models is trained using data supplied by a third-party data broker. The data broker does not reliably notify you about data-format changes. You want to make your model-training pipeline more robust against issues like this. What should you do?

options.text: Use TensorFlow Data Validation to detect and flag schema anomalies.
Use TensorFlow Transform to create a preprocessing component that will normalize data to the expected distribution, and replace values that don’t match the schema with 0.
Use tf.math to analyze the data, compute summary statistics, and flag statistical anomalies.
Use custom TensorFlow functions at the start of your model training to detect and flag known formatting errors.

questions.explanation:
TensorFlow Data Validation (TFDV) validates data statistics against a schema and identifies anomalies, including missing features, out-of-range values, and incorrect feature types. It is therefore suited to detecting unexpected source-data formatting changes before model training.

**Learn more:** [TensorFlow Data Validation](https://www.tensorflow.org/tfx/data_validation/install) · [TensorFlow Data Validation: Checking and analyzing your data](https://www.tensorflow.org/tfx/guide/tfdv)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You created a Vertex AI ML pipeline with preprocessing and training steps, with each set of steps running in its own custom Docker image. Your organization uses GitHub and GitHub Actions for CI/CD to execute unit and integration tests. You must automate the model-retraining workflow so it can be started both manually and when a new code version is merged into the main branch. You want to minimize the workflow-building steps while retaining maximum flexibility. How should you configure the CI/CD workflow?

options.text: Trigger a Cloud Build workflow to run tests, build custom Docker images, push the images to Artifact Registry, and launch the pipeline in Vertex AI Pipelines.
Trigger GitHub Actions to run the tests, launch a job on Cloud Run to build custom Docker images, push the images to Artifact Registry, and launch the pipeline in Vertex AI Pipelines.
Trigger GitHub Actions to run the tests, build custom Docker images, push the images to Artifact Registry, and launch the pipeline in Vertex AI Pipelines.
Trigger GitHub Actions to run the tests, launch a Cloud Build workflow to build custom Docker images, push the images to Artifact Registry, and launch the pipeline in Vertex AI Pipelines.

questions.explanation:
GitHub Actions can handle the manual and main-branch merge triggers and run the existing test suite. It can then invoke Cloud Build, whose build configuration can build the separate custom Docker images and publish them to Artifact Registry before a Vertex AI Pipeline run is launched. Cloud Build is designed for configurable container builds and Artifact Registry image publication; Cloud Run is not the service for building container images.

**Learn more:** [Build container images](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/building/build-containers) · [Cloud Build triggers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/build/docs/triggers)

questions.question: You are building a classification model to help predict your company’s various products. The dataset supplied for model development has class imbalance. You must minimize both false positives and false negatives. Which evaluation metric should you use to train the model appropriately?

options.text: F1 score
Recall
Accuracy
Precision

questions.explanation:
F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Precision penalizes false positives, while recall penalizes false negatives; therefore, F1 balances both error types and is more informative than accuracy for an imbalanced classification problem.\
\
**Learn more:** [scikit-learn f1_score documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.f1_score.html)

questions.domain: Collaborating within and across teams to manage data and models
questions.question: You are building a classification model to help predict your company’s various products. The dataset supplied for model development has class imbalance. You must minimize both false positives and false negatives. Which evaluation metric should you use to train the model appropriately?

options.text: Redaction, reproducibility, and explainability
Traceability, reproducibility, and explainability
Federated learning, reproducibility, and explainability
Differential privacy, federated learning, and explainability

questions.explanation:
Regulated, high-impact ML systems need traceability so their data, model versions, and outputs can be audited; reproducibility so results can be recreated and validated; and explainability so decision reasons can be understood and reviewed. Google Cloud guidance specifically calls for lineage and tracking to support regulatory compliance, and for comprehensive traceability, reproducibility, and explainability in trustworthy AI systems.

**Learn more:** [AI and ML perspective: Security](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/perspectives/ai-ml/security) · [AI and ML perspective: Reliability](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/perspectives/ai-ml/reliability)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to train a natural-language model for text classification on product descriptions containing millions of examples and 100,000 distinct words. You want to preprocess each word individually so it can be supplied to a recurrent neural network. What should you do?

options.text: Create a hot-encoding of words, and feed the encodings into your model.
Identify word embeddings from a pre-trained model, and use the embeddings in your model.
Sort the words by frequency of occurrence, and use the frequencies as the encodings in your model.
Assign a numerical value to each word from 1 to 100,000 and feed the values as inputs in your model.

questions.explanation:
Word embeddings represent words as compact dense vectors in which semantically related words can have related representations. An RNN can process the resulting sequence of vectors efficiently, whereas a 100,000-dimensional one-hot vector is sparse and costly, and a raw integer word ID or frequency does not convey semantic relationships.

**Learn more:** [TensorFlow: Word embeddings](https://www.tensorflow.org/text/guide/word_embeddings) · [TensorFlow: Text classification with an RNN](https://www.tensorflow.org/text/tutorials/text_classification_rnn)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to build a custom TensorFlow model for online predictions. The training data is stored in BigQuery. You need to apply instance-level data transformations for model training and serving, and you want to use the same preprocessing routine during both. How should you configure the preprocessing routine?

options.text: Create a BigQuery script to preprocess the data, and write the result to another BigQuery table.
Create a pipeline in Vertex AI Pipelines to read the data from BigQuery and preprocess it using a custom preprocessing component.
Create a preprocessing function that reads and transforms the data from BigQuery. Create a Vertex AI custom prediction routine that calls the preprocessing function at serving time.
Create an Apache Beam pipeline to read the data from BigQuery and preprocess it by using TensorFlow Transform and Dataflow.

questions.explanation:
TensorFlow Transform lets a single preprocessing definition be applied to training data and exported as a TensorFlow graph for inference serving. Running it in an Apache Beam pipeline on Dataflow supports scalable reads and preprocessing of BigQuery training data while keeping training and online-serving transformations consistent, avoiding training-serving skew.

**Learn more:** [The Transform TFX Pipeline Component](https://www.tensorflow.org/tfx/guide/transform) · [Preprocess data with TensorFlow Transform](https://www.tensorflow.org/tfx/tutorials/transform/simple?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an ML pipeline with Vertex AI Pipelines. You want the pipeline to upload a new version of an XGBoost model to Vertex AI Model Registry and deploy it to Vertex AI Endpoints for online inference. You want the simplest approach. What should you do?

options.text: Use the Vertex AI REST API within a custom component based on a vertex-ai/prediction/xgboost-cpu image
Use the Vertex AI ModelEvaluationOp component to evaluate the model
Use the Vertex AI SDK for Python within a custom component based on a python:3.10 image
Chain the Vertex AI ModelUploadOp and ModelDeployOp components together

questions.explanation:
`ModelUploadOp` is the prebuilt pipeline component for uploading a trained model to Vertex AI Model Registry, including uploading a version when a parent model is specified. It outputs a Vertex Model artifact that can be supplied directly to `ModelDeployOp` to deploy that model to a Vertex AI Endpoint for online inference.

**Learn more:** [Use Google Cloud Pipeline Components](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/use-components)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A production demand-forecasting pipeline uses Dataflow to preprocess raw data before model training and prediction. During preprocessing, it applies Z-score normalization to data stored in BigQuery and writes the results back to BigQuery. New training data is added every week.  
  
You want to improve efficiency by reducing computation time and manual intervention. What should you do?

options.text: Normalize the data using Google Kubernetes Engine.
Translate the normalization algorithm into SQL for use with BigQuery.
Use the normalizer_fn argument in TensorFlow's Feature Column API.
Normalize the data with Apache Spark using the Dataproc connector for BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery GoogleSQL provides aggregate functions such as `AVG` and standard-deviation functions, which can implement the Z-score calculation directly where the data resides. A scheduled BigQuery query can run recurrently and write the transformed data, eliminating unnecessary data movement and separate compute infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Aggregate functions | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/aggregate_functions) · [Scheduling queries | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/scheduling-queries)

questions.question: While monitoring GPU utilization during model training, you find that the implementation is natively synchronous. The training data is divided across multiple files. You want to decrease the execution time of the input pipeline. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the CPU load
Add caching to the pipeline
Increase the network bandwidth
Add parallel interleave to the pipeline

questions.explanation:
Parallel interleaving reads from multiple input files concurrently, overlapping file-opening and data-extraction work and reducing input-pipeline time. TensorFlow recommends `Dataset.interleave` with `num_parallel_calls` (often `tf.data.AUTOTUNE`) to parallelize reading from sharded input files.\
\
**Learn more:** [Better performance with the tf.data API](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/data_performance) · [Analyze tf.data performance with the TF Profiler](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/data_performance_analysis)

options.text: Comment out the part of the pipeline that you are not currently updating.
Enable caching in all the steps of the Kubeflow pipeline.
Delegate feature engineering to BigQuery and remove it from the pipeline.
Add a GPU to the model training step.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Pipelines execution caching reuses the outputs of a previous successful task when its cache key—based on its inputs, outputs, and component specification—matches. Matching tasks are skipped, so unchanged deterministic stages do not consume compute time or cost on subsequent development runs. [Configure execution caching](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/configure-caching)

**Learn more:** [Configure execution caching | Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/configure-caching)

A data science team is training a PyTorch image-classification model based on a pre-trained RestNet model. You need to conduct hyperparameter tuning to optimize several parameters. What should you do?

options.text: Convert the model to a Keras model, and run a Keras Tuner job.
Run a hyperparameter tuning job on AI Platform using custom containers.
Create a Kuberflow Pipelines instance, and run a hyperparameter tuning job on Katib.
Convert the model to a TensorFlow model, and run a hyperparameter tuning job on AI Platform.

questions.explanation:
Managed Google Cloud hyperparameter tuning can execute training trials in a custom container, so a PyTorch training application can retain its framework and dependencies while receiving trial-specific parameter values and reporting optimization metrics. Converting the model to Keras or TensorFlow is not required.

**Learn more:** [PyTorch integration | Vertex AI](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/start/pytorch) · [Create a hyperparameter tuning job | Vertex AI](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/samples/aiplatform-create-hyperparameter-tuning-job-sample)

questions.question: You are training an ML model on a large dataset and using a TPU to speed up the training process. You notice that training is taking longer than expected and discover that the TPU is not operating at full capacity. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the learning rate
Increase the number of epochs
Decrease the learning rate
Increase the batch size

questions.explanation:
Larger batch sizes generally improve TPU throughput and hardware utilization by providing enough parallel computation for the TPU cores. Google Cloud recommends using the largest batch size that fits in TPU memory; efficient batch sizes also reduce padding and memory-transfer inefficiencies.\
\
**Learn more:** [Cloud TPU performance guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/performance-guide) · [Troubleshooting TensorFlow - TPU](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/troubleshooting/trouble-tf)

questions.question: You are training an ML model on a large dataset and using a TPU to speed up the training process. You notice that training is taking longer than expected and discover that the TPU is not operating at full capacity. What should you do?

options.text: 1 = AI Platform, 2 = AI Platform, 3 = AutoML Vision
1 = AI Platform, 2 = AI Platform, 3 = AutoML Natural Language
1 = AI Platform, 2 = AI Platform, 3 = Cloud Natural Language API
1 = Cloud Natural Language API, 2 = AI Platform, 3 = Cloud Vision API

questions.explanation:
Ticket-priority classification and ticket-resolution-time regression need separately trained, task-specific models served from AI Platform endpoints. Sentiment analysis for general text is provided by the pre-trained Cloud Natural Language API, so a custom natural-language model is not needed when the tickets contain no domain-specific jargon.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Natural Language API — Analyzing Sentiment](https://docs.cloud.google.com/natural-language/docs/analyzing-sentiment) · [Vertex AI — Tabular Workflows](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/tabular-workflows/overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are training an object-detection machine learning model on a dataset comprising three million X-ray images, each approximately 2 GB in size. You use Vertex AI Training to run a custom training application on a Compute Engine instance with 32 cores, 128 GB of RAM, and one NVIDIA P100 GPU. You observe that model training is taking a very long time. You want to reduce training time without compromising model performance. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the instance memory to 512 GB and increase the batch size.
Replace the NVIDIA P100 GPU with a v3-32 TPU in the training job.
Enable early stopping in your Vertex AI Training job.
Use the tf.distribute.Strategy API and run a distributed training job.

questions.explanation:
Distributed data-parallel training uses multiple GPUs or machines to process portions of each batch concurrently and combines the gradients for synchronized model updates. TensorFlow's `tf.distribute.Strategy` supports this approach, and Vertex AI Training supports distributed TensorFlow jobs using distribution strategies such as `MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy`. Synchronous data parallelism preserves the same model-training objective and convergence behavior while reducing wall-clock time through additional compute resources.

**Learn more:** [Distributed training with TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/distributed_training) · [Distributed training on Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/distributed-training)

You are a data scientist at an industrial-equipment manufacturing company. You are building a regression model to estimate power consumption in the company’s manufacturing plants from sensor data collected across all plants. The sensors collect tens of millions of records each day. You must schedule daily training runs that use all data collected through the current date. You want the model to scale smoothly while requiring minimal development effort. What should you do?

options.text: Train a regression model using AutoML Tables.
Develop a custom TensorFlow regression model, and optimize it using Vertex AI Training.
Develop a custom scikit-learn regression model, and optimize it using Vertex AI Training.
Develop a regression model using BigQuery ML.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML creates and trains machine-learning models directly on data stored in BigQuery by using SQL, eliminating the need to move the growing sensor dataset into a separate training environment or to develop custom TensorFlow or scikit-learn code. It supports regression model types, including linear, boosted-tree, random-forest, DNN, and AutoML regressors, making it well suited to scheduled training on a very large tabular dataset.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery ML model creation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/model-overview) · [BigQuery ML CREATE MODEL statement](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/bigqueryml-syntax-create)

You need to design an architecture that provides asynchronous predictions to determine whether a specific mission-critical machine part will fail. Your system gathers data from multiple sensors on the machine. You want to build a model that predicts a failure in the next N minutes, based on the average of each sensor’s data from the previous 12 hours. How should you design the architecture?

options.text: 1. HTTP requests are sent by the sensors to your ML model, which is deployed as a microservice and exposes a REST API for prediction2. Your application queries a Vertex AI endpoint where you deployed your model.3. Responses are received by the caller application as soon as the model produces the prediction.

1. Events are sent by the sensors to Pub/Sub, consumed in real time, and processed by a Dataflow stream processing pipeline.2. The pipeline invokes the model for prediction and sends the predictions to another Pub/Sub topic.3. Pub/Sub messages containing predictions are then consumed by a downstream system for monitoring.

1. Export your data to Cloud Storage using Dataflow.2. Submit a Vertex AI batch prediction job that uses your trained model in Cloud Storage to perform scoring on the preprocessed data.3. Export the batch prediction job outputs from Cloud Storage and import them into Cloud SQL.

1. Export the data to Cloud Storage using the BigQuery command-line tool2. Submit a Vertex AI batch prediction job that uses your trained model in Cloud Storage to perform scoring on the preprocessed data.3. Export the batch prediction job outputs from Cloud Storage and import them into BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Streaming predictive-maintenance inference requires continuously ingesting sensor events, computing features over a rolling 12-hour window, and delivering predictions asynchronously. Pub/Sub supports decoupled event ingestion and downstream consumption, while a streaming Dataflow pipeline can process and transform the sensor stream, invoke model inference, and publish prediction messages for monitoring. Batch prediction workflows are not designed for this low-latency continuous use case, and synchronous REST serving does not provide the required asynchronous event-driven flow.

**Learn more:** [Dataflow and Vertex AI: Scalable and efficient model serving](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/streaming-prediction-with-dataflow-and-vertex) · [Dataflow: streaming analytics](https://cloud.google.com/products/dataflow)

You are on a team that develops state-of-the-art deep learning models using the TensorFlow framework. Your team conducts multiple ML experiments every week, making experiment runs hard to track. You want a straightforward way to efficiently track, visualize, and debug ML experiment runs on Google Cloud while minimizing overhead code. How should you proceed?

options.text: Set up Vertex AI Experiments to track metrics and parameters. Configure Vertex AI TensorBoard for visualization.
Set up a Cloud Function to write and save metrics files to a Cloud Storage bucket. Configure a Google Cloud VM to host TensorBoard locally for visualization.
Set up a Vertex AI Workbench notebook instance. Use the instance to save metrics data in a Cloud Storage bucket and to host TensorBoard locally for visualization.
Set up a Cloud Function to write and save metrics files to a BigQuery table. Configure a Google Cloud VM to host TensorBoard locally for visualization.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI Experiments organizes and compares ML experiment runs while recording parameters, summary metrics, and time-series metrics. Vertex AI TensorBoard is Google Cloud’s managed TensorBoard service for visualizing those metrics and inspecting training behavior, so it provides tracking and debugging without building custom metric-storage functions or operating a VM-hosted TensorBoard instance.

**Learn more:** [Configure your training script | Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/experiments/configure-training-script) · [Introduction to Vertex AI Experiments | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/experiments/intro-vertex-ai-experiments)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a model to help your company create more targeted online advertising campaigns. You need to build a dataset to train the model, while avoiding the creation or reinforcement of unfair bias in it. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Include a comprehensive set of demographic features
Include only the demographic groups that most frequently interact with advertisements
Collect a random sample of production traffic to build the training dataset
Collect a stratified sample of production traffic to build the training dataset
Conduct fairness tests across sensitive categories and demographics on the trained model

questions.explanation:
Stratified sampling draws data from each relevant subgroup, helping prevent demographic groups with lower production frequency from being underrepresented in the training dataset. Fairness tests across sensitive categories and demographics detect disparate model outcomes so bias can be identified and addressed. AWS documentation notes that insufficient representation of demographic groups in training data can cause biased model behavior, and that post-training bias metrics compare outcomes across demographic facets.

**Learn more:** [Amazon SageMaker AI: Pre-training Data Bias](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/clarify-detect-data-bias.html) · [Amazon SageMaker AI: Post-training Data and Model Bias Metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/clarify-measure-post-training-bias.html)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a real-time prediction engine that streams files, which might contain Personally Identifiable Information (PII), to Google Cloud. You plan to use the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP) API to scan the files. How should you make sure that unauthorized individuals cannot access the PII?

options.text: Stream all files to Google Cloud, and then write the data to BigQuery. Periodically conduct a bulk scan of the table using the DLP API.
Stream all files to Google Cloud, and write batches of the data to BigQuery. While the data is being written to BigQuery, conduct a bulk scan of the data using the DLP API.

Create two buckets of data: Sensitive and Non-sensitive. Write all data to the Non-sensitive bucket. Periodically conduct a bulk scan of that bucket using the DLP API, and move the sensitive data to the Sensitive bucket.

Create three buckets of data: Quarantine, Sensitive, and Non-sensitive. Write all data to the Quarantine bucket. Periodically conduct a bulk scan of that bucket using the DLP API, and move the data to either the Sensitive or Non-Sensitive bucket.

questions.explanation:
Unclassified incoming files should be stored in a restricted quarantine location until Sensitive Data Protection completes an inspection. Files can then be routed to Sensitive or Non-sensitive buckets with access controls appropriate to their classification, preventing general access to possible PII before it is identified.

**Learn more:** [Inspect Google Cloud storage and databases for sensitive data](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/inspecting-storage) · [Sensitive Data Protection overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/sensitive-data-protection-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must train an XGBoost model on a small dataset. Your training code has custom dependencies. You need to configure a Vertex AI custom training job and want to minimize training-job startup time while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a custom container that includes the data and the custom dependencies. In your training application, load the data into a pandas DataFrame and train the model.

Store the data in a Cloud Storage bucket, and use the XGBoost prebuilt custom container to run your training application. Create a Python source distribution that installs the custom dependencies at runtime. In your training application, read the data from Cloud Storage and train the model.

Use the XGBoost prebuilt custom container. Create a Python source distribution that includes the data and installs the custom dependencies at runtime. In your training application, load the data into a pandas DataFrame and train the model.

Store the data in a Cloud Storage bucket, and create a custom container with your training application and its custom dependencies. In your training application, read the data from Cloud Storage and train the model.

questions.explanation:
A custom container can include the training application and all required custom dependencies before the job runs, avoiding dependency installation during startup. Training data should be stored in Cloud Storage rather than packaged into the container; Google recommends using Cloud Storage or another Vertex AI-accessible storage service, ideally in the same project and region, to reduce latency.

**Learn more:** [Vertex AI custom containers overview](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/containers-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for an organization that operates a popular payment app. You created a fraudulent-transaction detection model with scikit-learn and deployed it to a Vertex AI endpoint. The endpoint currently uses 1 `e2-standard-2` machine with 2 vCPUs and 8 GB of memory. You find that gateway traffic fluctuates to as much as four times the endpoint's capacity. You need to resolve this issue using the most cost-effective approach. What should you do?

options.text: Re-deploy the model with a TPU accelerator.
Change the machine type to e2-highcpu-32 with 32 vCPUs and 32 GB of memory.
Set up a monitoring job and an alert for CPU usage. If you receive an alert, scale the vCPUs as needed.
Increase the number of maximum replicas to 6 nodes, each with 1 e2-standard-2 machine.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI endpoint autoscaling adds replicas as traffic rises, up to `maxReplicaCount`, and releases extra replicas as traffic falls. Retaining the small `e2-standard-2` machine type and allowing up to six replicas provides capacity for demand spikes while avoiding the continuous cost of a permanently oversized CPU machine or an unsuitable TPU accelerator.

**Learn more:** [AutomaticResources | Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/reference/rest/v1beta1/AutomaticResources) · [gcloud ai endpoints deploy-model | Google Cloud SDK Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/ai/endpoints/deploy-model)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a pet food company that operates an online forum. Customers upload photos of their pets to the forum to share with other users. About 20 photos are uploaded each day. You need to automatically detect, in near real time, whether every uploaded photo contains an animal. You want to prioritize speed and minimize the cost of application development and deployment. What should you do?

options.text: Send user-submitted images to the Cloud Vision API. Use object localization to identify all objects in the image and compare the results against a list of animals.
Download an object detection model from TensorFlow Hub. Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint. Send new user-submitted images to the model endpoint to classify whether each photo has an animal.

Manually label previously submitted images with bounding boxes around any animals. Build an AutoML object detection model by using Vertex AI. Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint Send new user-submitted images to your model endpoint to detect whether each photo has an animal.

Manually label previously submitted images as having animals or not. Create an image dataset on Vertex AI. Train a classification model by using Vertex AutoML to distinguish the two classes. Deploy the model to a Vertex AI endpoint. Send new user-submitted images to your model endpoint to classify whether each photo has an animal.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Vision API provides pre-trained image analysis, including object localization, which identifies detected objects and returns localized object annotations. Sending each uploaded image to this managed API and checking the detected objects against animal categories meets the near-real-time requirement without collecting labels, training a custom model, or deploying and maintaining a Vertex AI endpoint. Its per-image pricing also suits a low-volume workload.

**Learn more:** [Detect labels in an image by using the command line | Cloud Vision API](https://cloud.google.com/vision/docs/detect-labels-image-command-line) · [Cloud Vision pricing](https://cloud.google.com/vision/pricing)
