You have deployed a deep learning model to an Agent Platform endpoint using a machine type equipped with NVIDIA GPUs. You initially configured the endpoint's autoscaling to target 60% CPU utilization.  
  
During a load test, you observe the following:  
  
- Prediction latency increases significantly as traffic rises.  
- The number of replicas remains constant despite the increased load.  
- Cloud Monitoring shows CPU utilization staying below 40%.  
- Cloud Monitoring shows GPU utilization consistently exceeding 90%.  
  
You need to ensure the endpoint scales efficiently to handle the increased load. What should you do?

options.text: Update the autoscaling configuration to scale based on the GPU duty cycle metric.
Update the autoscaling configuration to decrease the target CPU utilization to 20%.
Redeploy the model to a machine type that includes a TPU.
Increase the minimum replica count for the endpoint to match the peak load that was observed during testing.

questions.explanation:
Because the workload is GPU-bound (GPU utilization over 90% while CPU stays under 40%), autoscaling that is based solely on CPU utilization cannot detect the real bottleneck and will not trigger additional replicas. Vertex AI (Agent Platform) online prediction endpoints support an autoscaling metric spec for the accelerator's duty cycle (aiplatform.googleapis.com/prediction/online/accelerator/duty_cycle), which reflects how busy the GPU actually is. Configuring the endpoint's autoscaling to scale on this GPU duty cycle metric allows the platform to add replicas in response to genuine GPU saturation, resolving the latency increase under load. Lowering the CPU target, moving to TPUs, or statically raising the minimum replica count do not address the mismatch between the autoscaling signal (CPU) and the actual resource constraint (GPU).

**Learn more:** [Scale inference nodes by using autoscaling | Vertex AI | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/autoscaling) · [Scale inference nodes by using autoscaling | Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/autoscaling)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company operates an ecommerce platform and maintains a large dataset of customer reviews, where each review is labeled as positive, negative, or neutral. You need to quickly prototype a sentiment analysis model that can accurately predict the sentiment labels for new customer reviews while keeping time and cost to a minimum. What should you do?

options.text: Use the Agent Platform Text Embeddings API to vectorize the text, and train a regression model by using Agent Platform AutoML to predict sentiment scores.
Use Agent Platform AutoML to train a multi-class classification model that predicts sentiment labels based on the training data.
Use the Natural Language API for real-time sentiment analysis.
Train a sentiment analysis model by using a BERT-based model, and fine-tune the model by using domain-specific customer reviews.

questions.explanation:
Since the reviews are already labeled with discrete sentiment categories (positive, negative, neutral), this is a multi-class text classification problem. AutoML is designed specifically to let teams quickly build accurate custom models from their own labeled datasets without needing to write custom training code, select architectures, or tune hyperparameters — minimizing both development time and cost while still training on the company's specific labeled data (unlike a generic pre-trained API) and without the added complexity or expense of manually fine-tuning a BERT-based model.

**Learn more:** [Evaluate and iterate AutoML text classification models | Vertex AI | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/text-data/classification/evaluate-model) · [Interpret prediction results from text sentiment analysis models](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/text-data/sentiment-analysis/interpret-results)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are an enterprise AI architect at a large international company. An ML team has asked for your help launching a pilot customer support bot. They plan to use the DeepSeek-V3.2 model and expect only a few hundred requests per day. You need to deploy the model quickly using a cost-efficient approach. What should you do?

options.text: Use the DeepSeek-V3.2 model as a service (MaaS) in Model Garden. Send HTTP requests in the Agent Platform endpoint using the Python requests library.

Download the DeepSeek-V3.2 binaries from Model Garden, and deploy the model on a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autoscaling cluster. Send HTTP requests to the GKE endpoint using the Python requests library.
Navigate to the DeepSeek-V3.2 model card in Model Garden. Click “Deploy model” to deploy it as an Agent Platform endpoint. Invoke the endpoint using the aiplatform SDK.
Use the DeepSeek-V3.2 model as a service (MaaS) in Model Garden. Use a Python client from the openai SDK, and pass a custom endpoint URL to the client.

questions.explanation:
Because the workload is a low-volume pilot, the most cost-efficient path is to consume DeepSeek-V3.2 as a Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) offering in Vertex AI Model Garden, which is billed per request/token and requires no infrastructure provisioning or management, unlike self-hosting the model on GKE or deploying it to a dedicated Vertex AI endpoint (both of which incur ongoing compute costs regardless of traffic). Vertex AI's MaaS models expose an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API, and the supported integration pattern is to use the `openai` Python SDK configured with a custom base URL pointing at the Vertex AI MaaS endpoint, rather than issuing raw HTTP requests.

Because the workload is GPU-bound (GPU utilization over 90% while CPU stays under 40%), autoscaling that is based solely on CPU utilization cannot detect the real bottleneck and will not trigger additional replicas. Vertex AI (Agent Platform) online prediction endpoints support an autoscaling metric spec for the accelerator's duty cycle (aiplatform.googleapis.com/prediction/online/accelerator/duty_cycle), which reflects how busy the GPU actually is. Configuring the endpoint's autoscaling to scale on this GPU duty cycle metric allows the platform to add replicas in response to genuine GPU saturation, resolving the latency increase under load. Lowering the CPU target, moving to TPUs, or statically raising the minimum replica count do not address the mismatch between the autoscaling signal (CPU) and the actual resource constraint (GPU).

You operate a high-traffic ecommerce application that relies on a recommendation model deployed on an Agent Platform endpoint. During flash sales, traffic spikes rapidly from 1,000 to 50,000 queries per second (QPS). During these spikes, the application returns 503: Service Unavailable errors because the autoscaler is unable to provision new resources quickly enough to meet the sudden surge in demand. You need to eliminate these service disruptions at the start of the sale. How should you configure the endpoint?

options.text: Change the machine type to an a2-highgpu-1g instance with an NVIDIA A100 GPU.
Increase the min_replica_count to a baseline that covers a significant portion of the expected spike, and set the max_replica_count to 100.
Set the min_replica_count to 1 and the max_replica_count to 100 in the deployed model’s automatic scaling configuration.
Deploy the model to a private Agent Platform endpoint, and autoscale based on GPU utilization.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI/Agent Platform endpoint autoscaling is reactive: it monitors utilization metrics and provisions additional replicas only after load increases, and spinning up new replicas (allocating compute, loading the model) takes time. When traffic jumps almost instantly by 50x, the autoscaler cannot keep pace, causing dropped requests (503 errors) during the ramp-up window. The correct mitigation is to increase the min_replica_count so that a substantial baseline of capacity is already running and ready to serve traffic before the spike hits, reducing the number of new replicas that must be provisioned reactively, while keeping max_replica_count high (e.g., 100) to handle any remaining growth beyond the baseline. This approach directly addresses the scale-up latency problem inherent to autoscaling, unlike simply changing the machine type, relying on default low min replicas, or switching to a private endpoint with GPU-based autoscaling.

**Learn more:** [Scale inference nodes by using autoscaling | Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/autoscaling)

You lead an ML team at a financial technology company. Your team is building a system to detect potentially fraudulent credit card transactions in real-time. The model must return a prediction with very low latency (under 200ms) to approve or deny the transaction. The system must also scale to handle millions of transactions per day. Your dataset consists of structured, tabular transaction data stored in BigQuery.  
  
Your team is proficient in data science but wants to avoid the complexity of managing and optimizing a real-time model serving infrastructure. What should you do?

options.text: In an Agent Platform Workbench notebook, build a deep neural network (DNN) using PyTorch. Provision a cluster of GPU-enabled Compute Engine instances, and create an API to serve the model for real-time predictions.
Use BigQuery ML to train a boosted tree classification model. Schedule a batch prediction job using the ML.PREDICT function that runs every minute and scores recent transactions.

Use Forecasting with Agent Platform AutoML to train a time-series model on the sequence of transactions. Deploy the model as a tabular workflow to predict which future time windows are likely to contain fraudulent activity.

Use Agent Platform AutoML to train using your tabular dataset from BigQuery. Deploy the trained model to an Agent Platform endpoint, and integrate the endpoint’s API into your transaction processing application.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI AutoML for tabular data lets you train directly on your BigQuery tabular dataset without writing custom modeling code, and once trained, you deploy the model to a fully managed Vertex AI endpoint. This endpoint provides low-latency online (synchronous) predictions and automatically handles autoscaling, load balancing, and infrastructure management, so the team never has to provision or tune servers, GPU clusters, or custom serving code — directly satisfying the sub-200ms latency requirement, the millions-of-transactions-per-day scale requirement, and the desire to avoid managing serving infrastructure. Batch prediction (as in option B) only returns results on a scheduled/batch basis and cannot meet a strict per-transaction real-time latency SLA. A custom DNN on self-managed GPU Compute Engine instances (option A) reintroduces exactly the infrastructure management burden the team wants to avoid. A forecasting time-series model (option C) is designed to predict values over future time windows, not to classify individual transactions as fraudulent in real time.

**Learn more:** [Vertex AI - AutoML tabular data overview](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/classification-regression/overview) · [Vertex AI - Get online (real-time) predictions](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/get-online-predictions)

You are training a ResNet-50 computer vision model on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform using a custom PyTorch container. The training job is configured with a generic machine type and one NVIDIA A100 GPU. While monitoring resource utilization during training, you notice the following:  
  
- GPU utilization is volatile, frequently dropping to 0% for short intervals  
- CPU utilization remains consistently above 90%  
  
You want to maximize GPU utilization in order to reduce training time. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the training batch size to saturate the GPU memory.
Update the DataLoader utility to increase the num_workers parameter and enable pin_memory.
Switch to a machine type with a higher number of GPUs, and implement the torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel strategy in the training code.
Enable automatic mixed precision (AMP) to speed up the matrix multiplications.

questions.explanation:
The pattern of near-idle GPU utilization combined with sustained high CPU usage indicates that the data loading and preprocessing pipeline running on the CPU cannot keep up with the GPU's compute speed, leaving the GPU starved for input batches. Increasing the DataLoader's num_workers parameter spawns additional worker processes to load and preprocess data in parallel, and enabling pin_memory=True speeds up host-to-device tensor transfers by using page-locked memory, allowing transfers to overlap with GPU computation. This directly addresses the data pipeline bottleneck and keeps the GPU fed continuously, improving utilization and reducing overall training time.

**Learn more:** [torch.utils.data — PyTorch documentation (DataLoader, num_workers, pin_memory)](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html) · [PyTorch Performance Tuning Guide](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/recipes/tuning_guide.html)

The team has decided to leverage LLMs available in Model Garden and wants to track model training artifacts. You need to figure out the best way to:  
  
- Share notebooks effectively within your team, and  
- Orchestrate the ML workflow  
  
while using Google-managed services as much as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Develop your code in Agent Platform Colab Enterprise, and orchestrate your ML workflow by using Agent Platform Pipelines.
Develop your code in Agent Platform Colab Enterprise, and orchestrate your ML workflow by using Cloud Workflows.
Develop your code in Agent Platform Workbench, and orchestrate your ML workflow by using Cloud Build.
Develop your code in Agent Platform Workbench, and orchestrate your ML workflow by using Agent Platform Pipelines.

questions.explanation: Colab Enterprise notebooks are designed for easy, IAM-based sharing across a team without requiring users to manage dedicated notebook compute infrastructure, unlike Workbench instances which are typically single-user and less convenient to share. For orchestrating the ML workflow, Vertex AI Pipelines (referred to here as Agent Platform Pipelines) is a fully managed, serverless pipeline orchestration service that also integrates with Vertex ML Metadata to automatically track model training artifacts and lineage—fulfilling both the orchestration and artifact-tracking requirements with fully managed Google Cloud services. Cloud Workflows and Cloud Build are general-purpose automation tools not tailored for ML pipeline orchestration or artifact lineage tracking, making them less suitable choices.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an ML workflow that preprocesses data, trains a model with hyperparameter tuning, and deploys the best model to an Agent Platform endpoint. Your preprocessing step takes two hours and outputs a 100 GB dataset. You run experiments daily using different model architectures, but always with the same preprocessing step.  
  
You need to automate this process and optimize the pipeline runs to minimize cost and time.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure an Agent Platform Pipelines workflow with a single component for the preprocessing and training steps. Use Agent Platform hyperparameter tuning jobs within the component to identify optimal parameters.

Configure an Agent Platform Pipelines workflow with separate components for the preprocessing and training steps. Enable caching on the preprocessing component, and use Agent Platform Serverless Training custom jobs for the training steps.

Configure an Agent Platform Pipelines workflow with separate components for the preprocessing and training steps. Use a Cloud Run function to trigger the pipeline, and configure Agent Platform Serverless Training custom jobs for the training steps.

Configure an Agent Platform Pipelines workflow that starts with an Agent Platform Serverless Training custom job for the preprocessing step. Use a Cloud Run function to launch the hyperparameter tuning job that is triggered when the preprocessed data arrives in Cloud Storage.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI (Agent Platform) Pipelines lets you define separate components for each pipeline step and supports execution caching: if a component's inputs haven't changed since a prior successful run, the pipeline service reuses the cached output instead of re-executing the component. Since the preprocessing step is identical across daily runs, splitting it into its own component and enabling caching avoids repeating the expensive two-hour preprocessing job and reprocessing the 100 GB dataset every time, directly reducing both cost and time. The training step, which varies daily by model architecture, should use Serverless (custom) Training jobs, which integrate with Vertex AI's hyperparameter tuning service to efficiently search for optimal parameters for each new architecture. Combining preprocessing and training into a single component (as in another option) would prevent caching from applying to just the static preprocessing step, while adding external triggers via Cloud Run functions is unnecessary complexity that doesn't address the core cost/time optimization need, which caching directly solves.

**Learn more:** [Build a pipeline - Vertex AI Pipelines caching](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/configure-caching) · [Create training pipelines](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/training/create-training-pipeline)

You are an ML engineer at a retail company. You need to automate a recurring retraining workflow for a demand forecasting model. The workflow spans dependencies across hybrid environments and must execute the following sequential steps:  
  
1. Trigger a shell script on an on-premises server to extract legacy sales data and send it to a Cloud Storage bucket.  
2. Trigger a pipeline in Agent Platform Pipelines to train and validate the new model.  
3. Push the validation metrics to a third-party API.  
  
You need a fully managed orchestration service that provides native connectors to handle these cross-platform dependencies. You want to use the most stable, robust solution. What should you do?

options.text: Use Workflows to define the orchestration logic in YAML. Use the http.post connector to trigger the on-premises shell script and the Agent Platform API for the training job.
Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Run function that executes the on-premises script using SSH, publishes a Pub/Sub message upon completion, and triggers the subsequent workflow steps.
Use Managed Service for Apache Airflow to define a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in Python. Use Apache Airflow operators and sensors to orchestrate the workflow steps.
Use Agent Platform Pipelines to develop a custom container component for each workflow step. Use the Kubeflow Pipelines (KFP) SDK to define the execution order.

questions.explanation:
Managed Service for Apache Airflow (Cloud Composer) is Google Cloud's fully managed workflow orchestration service specifically designed to coordinate complex, dependent tasks across hybrid environments, including on-premises systems, GCP services, and third-party APIs. It lets you define a DAG in Python and use mature, battle-tested Airflow operators and sensors (such as SSH operators to trigger on-prem scripts, GCS sensors to detect data landing in a bucket, Vertex AI operators to trigger and monitor training pipelines, and HTTP operators to call external APIs) to express sequential dependencies reliably. This makes it the most stable and robust option for orchestrating cross-platform ML retraining workflows, compared to lighter-weight tools like Workflows (limited native on-prem/complex dependency support), manually chained Cloud Scheduler/Cloud Run/Pub/Sub solutions (fragile, not a unified managed orchestrator), or Vertex AI Pipelines/KFP (scoped to ML pipeline steps rather than general cross-system orchestration).

**Learn more:** [Managed Airflow overview | Managed Service for Apache Airflow | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/composer/docs/composer-3/composer-overview) · [Managed Service for Apache Airflow | Apache Airflow 3](https://cloud.google.com/products/managed-service-for-apache-airflow)

You are building an automated training workflow with Agent Platform Pipelines. The pipeline trains a new custom model and registers it to Model Registry. You need to validate the model's performance on a held-out test dataset, and you want the model to be deployed to a production Agent Platform endpoint only if its evaluation metrics meet a specific threshold. You also want to minimize cost and administrative overhead.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the training component to calculate evaluation metrics on the training dataset during the training job. Output the metrics to the next step and use a conditional task to deploy the model if the evaluation metrics exceed the specified threshold.

Insert a Python component that pulls the latest model version from Model Registry. Compare its training metrics against the current production model, and use a conditional task to deploy the new model if it performs better.

Deploy the model to a temporary Agent Platform endpoint. Use a custom component to send the test dataset for online prediction, calculate the metrics, and deploy to the production endpoint if the evaluation metrics exceed the specified threshold.

Add a batch prediction component to generate predictions on the test dataset. Pass the results to a model evaluation component. Use a conditional task to deploy the model if the evaluation metrics exceed the specified threshold.

questions.explanation:
The recommended approach is to use a batch prediction component to run inference on the held-out test dataset, pass those results to a model evaluation component to compute the evaluation metrics, and then use a conditional (dsl.Condition) task that deploys the model to the production endpoint only when the metrics exceed the specified threshold. Batch prediction runs as a managed job without requiring a standing endpoint, which is far cheaper and simpler to administer than spinning up a temporary online endpoint (as in another option) or writing custom comparison logic in a Python component. Evaluating on the held-out test dataset (rather than the training dataset) is also required to get an unbiased measure of model performance, ruling out approaches that reuse training-time metrics.

**Learn more:** [Model evaluation components | Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/model-evaluation-component) · [BatchPredictionJob component | Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/batchprediction-component)

You are building a machine learning pipeline with the Kubeflow Pipelines (KFP) SDK that will run on Agent Platform Pipelines. The pipeline includes a preprocessing component that takes two hours to transform a large dataset.  
  
While iterating on the code for the subsequent `model_training` component, you need to resubmit the pipeline frequently for testing. You want the preprocessing component to only re-run if its inputs or parameters have changed, while minimizing effort, cost, and total execution time.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Ensure that execution caching is enabled for the preprocessing component by including the set_caching_options(enable_caching=True) method.
Track the run lineage using Agent Platform Experiments, and pass the output artifact URI from the previous run into the training component.
Configure the pipeline to write the preprocessed data to a persistent volume claim (PVC) that is shared across pipeline runs.
Add a dsl.Condition step to the pipeline that checks if the preprocessing step has executed in the last hour.

questions.explanation:
Agent Platform Pipelines (the current name for Vertex AI Pipelines, built on the KFP SDK) provides native execution caching. Each pipeline step's cache key is derived from the component's specification (container image, command, arguments) plus the actual input parameter values and input artifact IDs used for that run. When a pipeline is resubmitted, Agent Platform Pipelines checks Vertex ML Metadata for a prior execution with a matching cache key; if found, the cached outputs are reused and the step's execution is skipped entirely rather than being recomputed. Enabling this behavior for the preprocessing task via `set_caching_options(enable_caching=True)` ensures that as long as its inputs and parameters remain unchanged across pipeline resubmissions, the costly two-hour preprocessing step is skipped automatically, while unrelated changes to the `model_training` component (which has a different, changing specification) still trigger re-execution of just that component. This achieves the goal with minimal implementation effort, no added infrastructure, and directly ties re-execution to actual input/parameter changes, unlike manual lineage tracking, shared persistent volumes, or time-based conditional checks.

**Learn more:** [Configure execution caching | Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/machine-learning/pipelines/configure-caching) · [Use Caching | Kubeflow Pipelines](https://www.kubeflow.org/docs/components/pipelines/user-guides/core-functions/caching/)

You are an ML engineer at a large retail company. You have a BigQuery table containing five years of daily sales data for 50,000 distinct product SKUs. You need to generate a daily demand forecast for the next 30 days for each individual SKU.  
  
The solution must:  

- Automatically account for holidays and weekly seasonality.  
- Minimize data egress costs and operational complexity by keeping the data and model within the data warehouse.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use the CREATE MODEL... OPTIONS(model_type='ARIMA_PLUS') statement in BigQuery to generate a forecast based on historical SKU sales.
Use the gcloud ai custom-jobs create command to run a PyTorch LSTM container on Agent Platform that pulls data from a CSV into Cloud Storage.
Use the CREATE MODEL... OPTIONS(model_type='LINEAR_REG') statement in BigQuery to predict sales using the transaction date as a feature.
Use the google-cloud-aiplatform SDK to create a TimeSeriesDataset and trigger an AutoMLForecastingTrainingJob.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery ML's ARIMA_PLUS model type is designed for exactly this scenario. A single `CREATE MODEL ... OPTIONS(model_type='ARIMA_PLUS', time_series_id_col=..., time_series_timestamp_col=..., time_series_data_col=..., holiday_region=...)` statement can train separate but jointly-managed models for all 50,000 SKUs at once by specifying the SKU column as the `time_series_id_col`. The model automatically performs seasonal-trend decomposition (via STL/ETS) to capture weekly seasonality and can be configured with `holiday_region` to automatically adjust forecasts for holiday effects. Because training and inference (via `ML.FORECAST`) happen entirely inside BigQuery on the existing table, there is no need to export data to another service, minimizing both data egress costs and operational overhead compared to standing up a custom Vertex AI training job (option B) or using Vertex AI AutoML Forecasting (option D), which require moving data into a separate dataset/service. A simple linear regression on the date (option C) cannot model seasonality or holiday effects.

**Learn more:** [The CREATE MODEL statement for ARIMA_PLUS models | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/bigqueryml-syntax-create-time-series) · [Forecast multiple time series with an ARIMA_PLUS univariate model | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/arima-multiple-time-series-forecasting-tutorial)

You are working with a team building a real-time, personalized ad-ranking model. At request time, the model needs low-latency access to hundreds of user-level features. These features live in BigQuery and are updated frequently by a streaming Dataflow pipeline.  
  
As your user base keeps growing, you find that retrieving these features from BigQuery at request time pushes total inference latency past your 100 ms SLA.  
  
You need a feature-serving layer that:  
  
- Provides low-latency retrieval  
- Scales automatically  
- Minimizes operational overhead  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use the BigQueryReadClient to stream data directly into the model’s inference container.
Enable Agent Platform Feature Store, and use the FetchFeatureValues API to fetch features for the model.
Implement a Redis cache on Memorystore, and add a component to the Dataflow pipeline to write the feature to the Redis cache.
Use BigQuery BI Engine to accelerate the SQL queries used to fetch features.

questions.explanation:
A managed feature store with an online serving store is purpose-built for exactly this scenario: it stores frequently updated, entity-level features and exposes them through a low-latency retrieval API (FetchFeatureValues) so that features can be fetched at inference time well within tight SLAs such as 100 ms. Because it is a fully managed Google Cloud service, it scales automatically with request volume and removes the need to build, operate, or maintain custom caching infrastructure, satisfying both the low-latency and minimal-operational-overhead requirements. Streaming raw BigQuery reads (A) or accelerating BigQuery queries with BI Engine (D) do not achieve the sub-100ms single-entity lookup latency needed, and standing up a self-managed Redis cache on Memorystore (C) would require the team to build and operate custom pipeline components and cache-management logic, increasing operational overhead rather than minimizing it.

**Learn more:** [Online serving | Vertex AI Feature Store](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/featurestore/serving-online) · [Serve features from online store | Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/machine-learning/featurestore/latest/serve-feature-values)

You are optimizing the training of a 175-billion-parameter LLM on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. You have provisioned a TPU v5p Pod slice with 32 chips for the job. When you first ran the training using a standard data parallelism strategy, the job immediately failed with an out-of-memory (OOM) error. You need to implement a training strategy that resolves the memory issue while minimizing training latency. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the training to use a parameter server architecture where the model weights are stored in the host CPU memory.
Enable gradient checkpointing, and continue using the data parallelism strategy.
Configure the training to shard the model parameters and optimizer states, and continue using the data parallelism strategy.
Scale up the TPU Pod slice to include more chips, and continue using the data parallelism strategy.

questions.explanation:
Standard data parallelism replicates the entire model, its gradients, and its optimizer states on every chip, so for a 175B-parameter model the per-chip memory footprint (weights plus Adam-style optimizer states) vastly exceeds available HBM, causing an immediate OOM regardless of how many chips are added. The correct fix is to shard (partition) the model parameters and optimizer states across the chips in the pod slice — an approach analogous to Fully Sharded Data Parallelism/ZeRO — while still parallelizing over the data batch. This reduces the memory required per chip roughly by the sharding factor, resolves the OOM, and, because TPU pods have very high-bandwidth interconnects (ICI), the necessary all-gather/reduce-scatter communication for sharded parameters and states can be performed with minimal added latency compared to alternatives such as CPU-hosted parameter servers (host-device communication overhead) or pure gradient checkpointing (which only reduces activation memory, not parameter/optimizer memory, and adds recomputation cost).

**Learn more:** [Design training a Large Machine Learning Model on TPUs on GCP](https://medium.com/@gayathrikolluru1005/design-training-a-large-machine-learning-model-on-tpus-on-gcp-56a3c239e361) · [the world's largest distributed LLM training job on TPU v5e | Google Cloud Blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/the-worlds-largest-distributed-llm-training-job-on-tpu-v5e)

A custom classification model has been deployed to an Agent Platform endpoint to predict customer churn likelihood in real time. You need to gather the data required to compute the model's exact precision and recall by comparing the production predictions against ground truth data stored in BigQuery. You want to minimize development effort. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the prediction container to asynchronously write the prediction result to BigQuery after every request.
Schedule a daily Agent Platform batch prediction job that uses the same model resource as the deployed endpoint and stores predictions in BigQuery.
Update the model deployment parameters to enable request-response logging to BigQuery. Set the sampling rate to 1.0.
Create a model evaluation job by providing the model resource and the BigQuery ground truth table to calculate precision and recall.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI online prediction endpoints support a built-in request-response logging feature that can be enabled directly on the endpoint deployment configuration, writing every prediction request and its corresponding response to a specified BigQuery table without requiring any custom code. The logging sampling rate can be set anywhere from 0 to 1; setting it to 1.0 logs 100% of requests, which is necessary to compute exact (not sampled/estimated) precision and recall once the logged predictions are joined with the ground truth labels in BigQuery. This managed capability avoids the custom code changes needed to modify the serving container (which would be required for option A), avoids running a separate batch job that doesn't reflect the actual online serving path (option B), and differs from a model evaluation job, which is designed around static/batch evaluation datasets rather than continuously capturing live endpoint traffic (option D).

**Learn more:** [Log requests and responses | Generative AI on Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/multimodal/request-response-logging) · [Online prediction logging | Vertex AI | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/online-prediction-logging)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are in the exploratory phase of developing a demand forecasting model. Several terabytes of historical sales and inventory records are stored in a BigQuery table. You need to create a new, clean table to perform preliminary analyses on metrics such as:  
  
- Moving averages of sales figures  
- Weekly aggregates  
  
...all without additional data movement. You want to use the simplest approach and minimize overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Create a PreprocessingOp component in the Agent Platform Pipelines workflow to compute the moving averages and extract time-based features and write the processed data to a new destination table in BigQuery.

Read the data from BigQuery into a Dask DataFrame using Agent Platform Workbench. Perform exploratory data analysis (EDA) and feature engineering transformations, and write the processed data back to a new destination table in BigQuery.

Write a SQL query in the BigQuery console. Use the ML.TRANSFORM function in BigQuery ML to compute the moving averages and extract time-based features. Write the processed data to a new destination table in BigQuery.

Write a SQL query in the BigQuery console. Use standard SQL functions like CAST, EXTRACT, and window functions with OVER() clauses to perform the transformations and calculations. Materialize the results into a new destination table in BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Standard SQL in BigQuery already supports window functions (using the OVER() clause) along with functions like CAST and EXTRACT to compute moving averages, weekly aggregates, and time-based features directly on data residing in BigQuery. Writing a query that materializes the results into a new destination table keeps all processing inside BigQuery with no extra data movement, no additional infrastructure (such as pipelines or notebook compute), and no dependency on a machine learning model context, making it the simplest and lowest-overhead solution for exploratory analysis on a large existing table.

**Learn more:** [Window function calls | BigQuery | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/window-function-calls) · [ML.TRANSFORM function | BigQuery ML | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/bigqueryml-syntax-transform)

You work for a healthcare organization and need to automate the patient triage process. You want to build a telephony agentic solution using the Gemini Live API to conduct human-like conversations with patients and gather the necessary patient information.  
  
You plan to pilot the solution in Japanese. You need to:  
  
- Minimize latency  
- Minimize development time  
- Ensure high, native-like fluency in the model's responses  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Gemini Live API Speech-to-Text functionality to capture the user’s input followed by Text-to-Speech streaming processing with Chirp to communicate with the patient in their language.
Use the Gemini Live API, and configure the language_code field to ja-JP. Include a clear system instruction to respond in the patient’s language.
Fine-tune the Gemini Flash model on a dataset of Japanese medical transcripts to ensure native fluency. Deploy this custom model behind the Gemini Live API.
Use the Gemini Pro model to automatically select the appropriate language.

questions.explanation:
The Gemini Live API includes a speech configuration option that allows you to directly set the desired output language (via the language_code field, e.g., 'ja-JP') along with a system instruction directing the model to respond in that language. This uses the Live API's native audio generation capability, which produces low-latency, natural, native-sounding speech directly, without requiring a separate speech-to-text plus text-to-speech pipeline (which adds latency and complexity), without needing costly and time-consuming fine-tuning (which does not minimize development time), and without relying on automatic language detection (which does not guarantee consistent native fluency for the target language).

**Learn more:** [Get started with Live API | Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/live) · [Live API capabilities guide | Google AI for Developers](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/live-guide)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for an international bank. Your team is developing a generative AI application that summarizes complex financial reports. You need to implement an automated, scalable solution to evaluate and quantify the quality of generated summaries against the previous version of the solution.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Model Monitoring to track the prediction drift of the token output length.
Run an automatic side-by-side (AutoSxS) evaluation job in Agent Platform to compare outputs from the new and previous versions of the solution.

Deploy both versions of the solution, and use A/B testing to route a portion of production traffic to the new version and route the remaining traffic to the previous version. Compare user click-through rates.
Run an evaluation job in Agent Platform, and calculate a BLEU score to compare the new and previous versions of the solution.

questions.explanation:
AutoSxS (automatic side-by-side evaluation) is a pairwise, model-based evaluation pipeline that automatically compares outputs generated by two different models or solution versions for the same inputs. It uses an autorater to judge which output is better, producing example-level judgments and aggregate win-rate metrics, without requiring manual human review for every comparison. This makes it an automated and scalable way to quantify quality differences between the new and previous versions of a summarization solution — exactly the requirement described. Monitoring token length drift does not assess summary quality; A/B testing with click-through rate measures user engagement rather than content quality; and BLEU scoring is a simpler n-gram overlap metric that is less suited to evaluating nuanced summarization quality compared to the purpose-built pairwise evaluation pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Run AutoSxS pipeline to perform pairwise model-based evaluation | Generative AI on Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/generative-ai/models/side-by-side-eval) · [Run AutoSxS pipeline to perform pairwise model-based evaluation | Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/side-by-side-eval)

You are building a conversational agent using generative AI to help bank customers with questions about their products and transaction history. You need to make sure the agent's responses never include personally identifiable information (PII), and you want to achieve this with the least amount of effort. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the safety_settings thresholds within the Agent Platform model parameters to Block_Most.

questions.explanation:
Model Armor, when integrated with Sensitive Data Protection (Cloud DLP), provides a managed, out-of-the-box capability to inspect and redact over 150 types of sensitive data—including PII such as names, account numbers, and other identifiers—from both prompts sent to and responses generated by an LLM-based agent. This requires only configuring a Model Armor template linked to Sensitive Data Protection, rather than writing and maintaining custom detection logic. Safety_settings thresholds (option A) govern harmful content categories like hate speech or harassment, not PII. A custom regex-based wrapper (option B) demands significant development effort and only covers a single narrow PII pattern, leaving many other PII types undetected. SHAP values (option D) are used for model explainability and feature attribution, not for identifying or redacting sensitive data in generated text.

**Learn more:** [Model Armor overview | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview) · [How Model Armor can help protect your AI apps | Google Cloud Blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/how-model-armor-can-help-protect-your-ai-apps)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are working for a media company and building a solution that needs to transcribe and diarize (identify speakers in) live audio streams in near real-time. The solution uses an optimized WhisperX model built on PyTorch, which relies on several libraries and weights obtained from the Hugging Face Hub. The deployment must also include proprietary Python post-processing logic — covering speaker diarization and alignment correction — that runs immediately after model inference.  
  
Given that the solution must be efficient, scalable, support high throughput, and keep serving latency to a minimum, which deployment approach should you use for this model and its associated logic?

options.text: Deploy the WhisperX model artifacts to an Agent Platform endpoint using a pre-built PyTorch serving container configured with a GPU. Host the custom post-processing scripts in a Cloud Run function that receives the endpoint’s prediction output and performs the final diarization.

Use a self-managed Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster for deployment. Package the model and logic into a container, and configure the cluster’s horizontal pod autoscaler (HPA) to manage throughput.

Package the WhisperX model artifacts, the specific Python post-processing scripts, and the necessary dependencies (including Hugging Face libraries) into a single, custom serving container image. Deploy this custom image to a GPU-enabled Agent Platform endpoint.

Locate the WhisperX model in the Model Garden and use the “1-click deploy” feature to deploy it to an Agent Platform endpoint. Route the output to a Dataflow pipeline that uses a custom DoFn function to handle the post-processing and logging.

questions.explanation:
Vertex AI (Agent Platform) custom containers let you bundle the model artifacts, all required dependencies (including Hugging Face libraries), and custom pre/post-processing code into a single container image that implements the platform's prediction protocol. Deploying that single container to a GPU-enabled endpoint keeps inference and the proprietary post-processing (diarization and alignment correction) in the same process, eliminating the extra network round trip and serialization overhead that would be introduced by routing predictions to a separate service such as Cloud Run or a Dataflow pipeline. This also avoids the operational burden of managing a self-hosted Kubernetes cluster, while still benefiting from the managed endpoint's autoscaling and GPU support — satisfying the requirements for efficiency, scalability, high throughput, and minimal latency.

**Learn more:** [Custom containers for prediction | Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/predictions/use-custom-container)

You have deployed a conversational application that uses Gemini. You recently collected thousands of rows of user feedback about the verbosity and accuracy of the model's responses. The feedback indicates that:  
  
- The responses are factually correct.  
- Users want different levels of verbosity depending on the type of question.  
  
You need to adjust the model so that its responses are more consistent with users' expectations. You want a solution that is scalable and minimizes application maintenance.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Experiment with other models in Model Garden. Perform A/B testing by setting each model as your application’s default model. Choose a model based on the results.

Ask users to indicate all scenarios where they expect concise responses versus verbose responses. Modify the application’s prompt to include these scenarios and their respective verbosity levels. Re-evaluate the verbosity of responses with updated prompts.

Implement a keyword-based routing layer. If the user’s input contains the words “detailed” or “description,” return a verbose response. If the user’s input contains the word “fact,” re-prompt Gemini to summarize the response and return a concise response.

Ask users to provide examples of responses with the appropriate verbosity as a list of question and answer pairs. Use this dataset to perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in Agent Platform. Re-evaluate the verbosity of responses with the tuned version.

questions.explanation: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) allows you to use the collected feedback — reformatted as question/answer pairs that demonstrate the desired verbosity for different question types — to adjust the model's behavior directly. This approach scales with the volume of feedback data and does not require ongoing manual updates to prompts or brittle keyword-matching logic, unlike manually enumerating scenarios in the prompt or building a keyword-based routing layer, both of which require continual maintenance as new question types emerge. Switching to a different foundation model via A/B testing does not use the specific feedback data collected and does not guarantee alignment with the verbosity expectations captured in that feedback.

You manage an ML workflow for a fraud detection model. The source code for data processing and model training is stored in a version control repository.  
  
You need to implement a continuous training (CT) pipeline that automatically:  
  
- Runs unit tests  
- Launches a new training run on Agent Platform Pipelines  
  
whenever code is updated in the repository. You want to use a fully managed service to orchestrate this process.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Run function that is triggered by repository commits. The function runs the unit tests, launches a custom training job, and uses Model Monitoring to validate the new model’s performance before deployment.

Define a Cloud Workflow to monitor the repository for changes. Configure the workflow on Agent Platform Pipelines to orchestrate and run the unit tests. Use the model evaluation component to validate the new model’s performance before deployment.
Configure Agent Platform Pipelines to poll the repository for updates. Add a conditional step in the pipeline that uses Model Monitoring to validate the new model’s performance before deployment.

Create a Cloud Build trigger associated with the repository. Define a build configuration file that runs the unit tests and triggers a job on Agent Platform Pipelines. Use the model evaluation component to validate the model performance before deployment.

questions.explanation:
The recommended pattern for CI/CT on Google Cloud is to use Cloud Build, a fully managed CI/CD service, with a trigger bound to the source repository so that every commit automatically kicks off a build. The build configuration file (cloudbuild.yaml) runs the unit tests and, on success, submits/launches a new run on the managed pipeline orchestrator (Vertex AI/Agent Platform Pipelines). Within that pipeline, the model evaluation component is the correct mechanism to validate the new model's performance against a baseline before it is promoted for deployment — Model Monitoring is designed for detecting training-serving skew and drift on an already-deployed model, not for pre-deployment evaluation gating. This trigger-driven, managed-build-then-managed-pipeline approach avoids custom polling or monitoring logic and matches Google's documented continuous training reference architecture.

**Learn more:** [Build a pipeline for continuous model training | Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/continuous-training-tutorial) · [GitHub - GoogleCloudPlatform/mlops-with-vertex-ai](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/mlops-with-vertex-ai)

You are deploying a generative AI chatbot for an online gaming community using Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. During beta testing, you find that users can submit malicious prompts that cause the model to generate hate speech and violent content. You need to add a guardrail to block this content in production while keeping development effort to a minimum.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Update the system instruction (system prompt) of the model to explicitly state: “You are a helpful assistant. Do not generate hate speech or violent content.”
Implement and configure Model Armor to sanitize responses if hateful content is detected.
Create a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) job in Agent Platform, and tune the model using a curated dataset of safe, policy-compliant gaming conversations.
Integrate the Cloud Natural Language API’s moderation capabilities to analyze and block toxic user prompts before they reach the chatbot model.

questions.explanation:
Model Armor is Google Cloud's purpose-built service for runtime protection of generative AI applications. It screens both incoming user prompts and outgoing model responses, detecting and blocking harmful content categories such as hate speech, harassment, violent content, and sexually explicit material, with adjustable confidence thresholds to tune enforcement to the application's risk tolerance. It has a native, low-effort integration path with Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, where interactions between users, agents, and the underlying LLM are routed through Model Armor so both prompts and responses are inspected before being surfaced to the user—achieving the required guardrail with minimal custom development. In contrast, editing the system prompt is easily bypassed by adversarial inputs, fine-tuning requires substantial data curation and engineering effort, and the Cloud Natural Language API's moderation features are not the integrated safety mechanism for this platform.

**Learn more:** [Model Armor overview | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview) · [Integration with Gemini Enterprise | Model Armor | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/model-armor-agentspace-integration)
